topics.title: Web Fundamentals
topics.contentHtml:
Web Fundamentals for .NET Developers

A practical guide to understanding how your Blazor Server app serves content.

Table of Contents

  1. Static vs Dynamic Content
  2. The wwwroot Folder
  3. Kestrel Web Server
  4. Browser Caching
  5. Cache Busting
  6. The Request Pipeline

Static vs Dynamic Content

Static Files

Files served exactly as they are on disk. No code runs, no database queries, no user-specific changes.

File Type Examples Characteristics
JavaScript .js Browser executes client-side
Stylesheets .css Browser applies styles
Images .png, .jpg, .svg Browser displays
Fonts .woff2, .ttf Browser renders text
Documents .pdf, .html Browser displays/downloads

Dynamic Content

Content generated by code at request time. Can vary by user, time, database state, etc.

Source Examples Characteristics
Razor Components .razor C# code generates HTML
API Controllers /api/* C# returns JSON/data
Razor Pages .cshtml C# + HTML templating

Key Insight

Static:  Browser asks for /js/app.js → Server sends file bytes → Done
Dynamic: Browser asks for /dashboard → Server runs C# → Queries DB → Renders HTML → Sends result

The wwwroot Folder

The wwwroot folder is special in ASP.NET Core. It's the only folder that's publicly accessible by default.

Structure

YourProject/
├── wwwroot/                 ← PUBLIC (accessible via HTTP)
│   ├── js/
│   │   └── script.js        → GET /js/script.js
│   ├── css/
│   │   └── app.css          → GET /css/app.css
│   ├── images/
│   │   └── logo.png         → GET /images/logo.png
│   └── favicon.ico          → GET /favicon.ico
│
├── Pages/                   ← PRIVATE (not directly accessible)
├── Services/                ← PRIVATE
├── Models/                  ← PRIVATE
└── appsettings.json         ← PRIVATE (never expose!)

URL Mapping

The wwwroot folder itself is not part of the URL:

File Path URL
wwwroot/js/app.js /js/app.js
wwwroot/css/site.css /css/site.css
wwwroot/images/photo.png /images/photo.png

Security Note

Never put sensitive files in wwwroot:

  • ❌ appsettings.json
  • ❌ .env files
  • ❌ Connection strings
  • ❌ API keys
  • ❌ Source code (.cs, .razor)

Kestrel Web Server

What is Kestrel?

Kestrel is the built-in web server that comes with .NET. It's not a physical machine—it's software that runs inside your application.

Architecture Layers

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Physical Machine (your PC, cloud VM, container)            │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Operating System (Windows, Linux, macOS)              │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │ │
│  │  │  Your Application (dotnet run / HRModule.exe)    │  │ │
│  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │ │
│  │  │  │  Kestrel Web Server                        │  │  │ │
│  │  │  │  • Listens on ports (5000, 5001, 80, 443)  │  │  │ │
│  │  │  │  • Receives HTTP/HTTPS requests            │  │  │ │
│  │  │  │  • Routes to middleware pipeline           │  │  │ │
│  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When You Run dotnet run

  1. Your application starts
  2. Kestrel initializes inside your app
  3. Kestrel binds to configured ports (e.g., https://localhost:5001)
  4. Kestrel waits for incoming HTTP requests
  5. Each request flows through the middleware pipeline

Production Considerations

In production, Kestrel often sits behind a reverse proxy:

Internet → Nginx/IIS/Azure → Kestrel → Your App
           (reverse proxy)    (app server)

The reverse proxy handles:

  • SSL termination
  • Load balancing
  • Request buffering
  • Static file caching

Browser Caching

Why Browsers Cache

Downloading files is slow and uses bandwidth. Browsers store copies locally to:

  • Speed up page loads
  • Reduce server load
  • Save user bandwidth

How Caching Works

First Visit:
  Browser: GET /js/script.js
  Server:  200 OK + file contents + Cache-Control: max-age=3600
  Browser: Saves file with URL as key

Second Visit (within 1 hour):
  Browser: Checks cache for /js/script.js
  Browser: Found! Uses cached version (no network request)

Cache Headers

Servers control caching via HTTP headers:

Header Example Meaning
Cache-Control max-age=31536000 Cache for 1 year
Cache-Control no-cache Always revalidate with server
Cache-Control no-store Never cache
ETag "abc123" File fingerprint for validation
Last-Modified Wed, 01 Jan 2025 When file last changed

The Problem

When you update script.js on the server:

  • Server has: New version
  • Browser has: Old cached version
  • Browser doesn't know to fetch new version!

Cache Busting

The Solution

Trick the browser into thinking it's a different file.

Method 1: Query String (Simple)

<!-- Before update -->
<script src="/js/script.js?v=1"></script>

<!-- After update -->
<script src="/js/script.js?v=2"></script>

How it works:

  • Browser sees /js/script.js?v=1 and /js/script.js?v=2 as different URLs
  • Server ignores ?v=2 and serves the same file
  • Browser downloads fresh copy and caches under new URL

Pros: Simple, no build tools needed Cons: Manual version incrementing

Method 2: File Hash (Production)

Build tools generate unique filenames based on file content:

<!-- Before update -->
<script src="/js/script.a1b2c3.js"></script>

<!-- After update (content changed, hash changed) -->
<script src="/js/script.d4e5f6.js"></script>

Pros: Automatic, optimal caching (cache forever, new content = new URL) Cons: Requires build tooling (webpack, esbuild, etc.)

Method 3: ASP.NET Core Tag Helper

<script src="~/js/script.js" asp-append-version="true"></script>

Renders as:

<script src="/js/script.js?v=SHA256HashOfFile"></script>

Pros: Automatic, built into ASP.NET Core Cons: Only works in Razor views/pages

The Request Pipeline

Middleware Concept

ASP.NET Core processes requests through a pipeline of middleware. Each middleware can:

  1. Handle the request and return a response
  2. Pass the request to the next middleware
  3. Do something before AND after the next middleware

Visual Pipeline

Request                                                    Response
   │                                                          ▲
   ▼                                                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UseHttpsRedirection()                                       │
│  Redirects HTTP → HTTPS                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   │                                                          ▲
   ▼                                                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UseStaticFiles()                                            │
│  If URL matches wwwroot file → serve it → STOP               │
│  Otherwise → pass to next middleware                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   │                                                          ▲
   ▼                                                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UseRouting()                                                │
│  Determines which endpoint matches the URL                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   │                                                          ▲
   ▼                                                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UseAuthentication() / UseAuthorization()                    │
│  Validates user identity and permissions                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   │                                                          ▲
   ▼                                                          │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MapBlazorHub() / MapControllers() / MapRazorPages()         │
│  Your application code runs here                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Static Files Example

GET /js/face/script.js

1. UseHttpsRedirection: "Already HTTPS, pass through"
2. UseStaticFiles: "Checking wwwroot/js/face/script.js..."
   Found! Read file, send to browser, DONE.
   (Later middleware never runs)

GET /dashboard

1. UseHttpsRedirection: "Already HTTPS, pass through"
2. UseStaticFiles: "Checking wwwroot/dashboard..."
   Not found. Pass to next middleware.
3. UseRouting: "Matches Blazor route /dashboard"
4. UseAuthentication: "User is logged in"
5. UseAuthorization: "User has permission"
6. MapBlazorHub: Render Dashboard.razor component

Order Matters!

// Program.cs - ORDER IS CRITICAL

app.UseHttpsRedirection();     // 1. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS first
app.UseStaticFiles();          // 2. Serve static files (fast path)
app.UseRouting();              // 3. Match routes
app.UseAuthentication();       // 4. Who is the user?
app.UseAuthorization();        // 5. Can they access this?
app.MapBlazorHub();            // 6. Handle Blazor
app.MapFallbackToPage("/_Host"); // 7. Fallback for SPA routing

If you put UseAuthentication() before UseStaticFiles(), you'd require login to see CSS/JS files!

Quick Reference

Common Paths

What Path
Static files root wwwroot/
JavaScript wwwroot/js/
CSS wwwroot/css/
Images wwwroot/images/

Common Issues

Problem: CSS/JS changes not appearing Solution: Cache busting (?v=2) or hard refresh (Ctrl+F5)

Problem: 404 for static files Solution: Check file exists in wwwroot/, check app.UseStaticFiles() is called

Problem: Static files require authentication Solution: Ensure UseStaticFiles() comes before UseAuthentication()

Further Reading

  • ASP.NET Core Static Files
  • ASP.NET Core Middleware
  • Kestrel Web Server

topics.title: C# Generics — Complete Guide
topics.contentHtml:
Generics in C#

A Comprehensive Guide

Part I: Historical Context

Chapter 1: The World Before Generics

1.1 The Problem of Type Safety

Before generics were introduced, developers faced a fundamental tension in programming: flexibility versus type safety.

Imagine you're building a collection to store items. You want it to be reusable—capable of storing integers today, strings tomorrow, and custom Employee objects next week. In the early days of C# (versions 1.0 and 1.1), you had two imperfect options.

Option A: Create Type-Specific Collections

public class IntegerList
{
    private int[] _items;
    public void Add(int item) { /* ... */ }
    public int Get(int index) { /* ... */ }
}

public class StringList
{
    private string[] _items;
    public void Add(string item) { /* ... */ }
    public string Get(int index) { /* ... */ }
}

public class EmployeeList
{
    private Employee[] _items;
    public void Add(Employee item) { /* ... */ }
    public Employee Get(int index) { /* ... */ }
}

This approach provided type safety—the compiler would catch errors like adding a string to an IntegerList. However, it was utterly impractical. For every type you needed to store, you had to write an entirely new collection class. Code duplication ran rampant.

Option B: Use System.Object

The .NET Framework offered a seemingly elegant solution: since every type in .NET inherits from System.Object, you could create a single collection that stores objects:

public class ArrayList
{
    private object[] _items;
    
    public void Add(object item) { /* ... */ }
    public object Get(int index) { /* ... */ }
}

This was the approach taken by System.Collections.ArrayList, and it worked—sort of. You could store anything:

ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(42);
list.Add("Hello");
list.Add(new Employee("Alice"));

But this flexibility came at a severe cost.

1.2 The Two Penalties of Object-Based Collections

Penalty #1: Boxing and Unboxing (Performance)

In .NET, types are divided into two categories:

  • Value types (e.g., int, double, bool, struct) — stored directly on the stack
  • Reference types (e.g., string, classes) — stored on the heap, with a reference on the stack

When you store a value type in an object-based collection, the runtime must perform boxing: wrapping the value in an object on the heap.

ArrayList numbers = new ArrayList();
numbers.Add(42);  // Boxing occurs here: int → object

When retrieving, unboxing occurs:

int value = (int)numbers[0];  // Unboxing: object → int

Boxing and unboxing are expensive operations. They involve:

  • Memory allocation on the heap
  • Copying data between stack and heap
  • Additional garbage collection pressure

In tight loops processing thousands of items, this overhead was devastating to performance.

Penalty #2: Loss of Type Safety (Correctness)

With object-based collections, the compiler had no way to enforce what types were stored:

ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(1);
list.Add(2);
list.Add("three");  // Compiles fine!

foreach (object item in list)
{
    int number = (int)item;  // Runtime exception on "three"!
}

Errors that should have been caught at compile time now exploded at runtime—sometimes in production, sometimes in edge cases that testing missed. This violated a core principle of strongly-typed languages: catch errors as early as possible.

1.3 The Industry Response

The limitations of object-based collections were not unique to C#. The Java community faced identical challenges, and in 2004, Java 5.0 introduced generics. C++ had long offered templates, a compile-time mechanism for generic programming.

Microsoft and the C# team, led by Anders Hejlsberg, recognized that a robust generics implementation was essential. However, they made a crucial design decision that differentiated C# generics from Java's approach.

Part II: The Advent of Generics

Chapter 2: Generics Arrive in C# 2.0

In November 2005, C# 2.0 was released alongside .NET Framework 2.0. Generics were the flagship feature.

2.1 The Core Concept

A generic is a type or method that is parameterized by one or more type parameters. Instead of committing to a specific type, you define a "placeholder" that gets filled in when the generic is used.

public class List<T>
{
    private T[] _items;
    
    public void Add(T item) { /* ... */ }
    public T Get(int index) { /* ... */ }
}

The <T> is a type parameter. By convention:

  • T — Type (general purpose)
  • TKey, TValue — for key-value scenarios
  • TInput, TOutput — for transformation scenarios
  • TEntity — for entity/model scenarios

When you use the generic, you provide a type argument:

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
List<string> names = new List<string>();
List<Employee> employees = new List<Employee>();

Each of these is a constructed type—a specific version of the generic with concrete types substituted for the parameters.

2.2 The Benefits Realized

Benefit #1: Type Safety Restored

The compiler now enforces type correctness:

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
numbers.Add(1);
numbers.Add(2);
numbers.Add("three");  // Compile error! Cannot convert string to int

Errors are caught immediately, in your IDE, before the code ever runs.

Benefit #2: No Boxing for Value Types

The .NET runtime generates specialized versions of generic types for value types. When you use List<int>, the runtime creates a version that works directly with integers—no boxing required.

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
numbers.Add(42);  // No boxing! Stored directly as int
int value = numbers[0];  // No unboxing! Retrieved directly as int

Performance-critical code could now use collections without the overhead.

Benefit #3: Code Reuse Without Sacrifice

A single generic class serves infinite use cases:

// One implementation, infinite applications
List<int> integers = new List<int>();
List<string> strings = new List<string>();
List<Customer> customers = new List<Customer>();
List<List<int>> matrix = new List<List<int>>();  // Generics can nest!

2.3 Reification: C#'s Secret Weapon

Here lies a critical distinction between C# and Java generics.

Java uses type erasure: generic type information exists only at compile time. At runtime, a List<String> and a List<Integer> are both just List. This was done for backward compatibility with older JVMs but limits what generics can do.

C# uses reification: generic type information is preserved at runtime. The CLR (Common Language Runtime) knows the difference between List<int> and List<string>. This enables:

// You can check generic types at runtime
Type listType = typeof(List<int>);
Console.WriteLine(listType.IsGenericType);  // True
Console.WriteLine(listType.GetGenericArguments()[0]);  // System.Int32

// You can create generic types dynamically
Type openType = typeof(List<>);
Type closedType = openType.MakeGenericType(typeof(string));
object instance = Activator.CreateInstance(closedType);

This design decision makes C# generics more powerful and enables sophisticated scenarios in frameworks like Entity Framework, dependency injection containers, and serialization libraries.

Part III: Mastering Generic Syntax

Chapter 3: Generic Classes and Structures

3.1 Defining a Generic Class

Let's build a practical example—a generic Result<T> type for handling operation outcomes:

public class Result<T>
{
    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    public T Value { get; }
    public string Error { get; }
    
    private Result(bool isSuccess, T value, string error)
    {
        IsSuccess = isSuccess;
        Value = value;
        Error = error;
    }
    
    public static Result<T> Success(T value)
    {
        return new Result<T>(true, value, null);
    }
    
    public static Result<T> Failure(string error)
    {
        return new Result<T>(false, default, error);
    }
}

Usage:

public Result<Employee> GetEmployee(int id)
{
    var employee = _database.Find(id);
    
    if (employee == null)
        return Result<Employee>.Failure("Employee not found");
    
    return Result<Employee>.Success(employee);
}

// Calling code
var result = GetEmployee(42);
if (result.IsSuccess)
{
    Console.WriteLine(result.Value.Name);
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine(result.Error);
}

3.2 Multiple Type Parameters

Generics can have multiple type parameters:

public class Pair<TFirst, TSecond>
{
    public TFirst First { get; set; }
    public TSecond Second { get; set; }
    
    public Pair(TFirst first, TSecond second)
    {
        First = first;
        Second = second;
    }
}

// Usage
var pair = new Pair<string, int>("Age", 30);
var coordinate = new Pair<double, double>(45.5, 122.7);

The System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<TKey, TValue> is a prime example from the framework.

3.3 Generic Structs

Value types can also be generic:

public struct Point<T>
{
    public T X { get; }
    public T Y { get; }
    
    public Point(T x, T y)
    {
        X = x;
        Y = y;
    }
}

// Usage
Point<int> pixelPoint = new Point<int>(100, 200);
Point<double> precisePoint = new Point<double>(3.14159, 2.71828);

Chapter 4: Generic Methods

4.1 Methods with Type Parameters

Methods can be generic independently of their containing class:

public class Utilities
{
    public static void Swap<T>(ref T a, ref T b)
    {
        T temp = a;
        a = b;
        b = temp;
    }
}

// Usage
int x = 5, y = 10;
Utilities.Swap<int>(ref x, ref y);  // x = 10, y = 5

string first = "Hello", second = "World";
Utilities.Swap<string>(ref first, ref second);  // Swapped!

4.2 Type Inference

The compiler can often infer type arguments:

int x = 5, y = 10;
Utilities.Swap(ref x, ref y);  // Compiler infers <int>

string a = "Hello", b = "World";
Utilities.Swap(ref a, ref b);  // Compiler infers <string>

This makes generic methods feel as natural as non-generic ones.

4.3 Generic Methods in Non-Generic Classes

A common pattern in utility classes:

public static class CollectionExtensions
{
    public static bool IsEmpty<T>(this ICollection<T> collection)
    {
        return collection == null || collection.Count == 0;
    }
    
    public static T FirstOrDefault<T>(this IEnumerable<T> source, T defaultValue)
    {
        foreach (T item in source)
            return item;
        return defaultValue;
    }
}

// Usage
List<int> numbers = new List<int>();
bool empty = numbers.IsEmpty();  // True

int first = numbers.FirstOrDefault(-1);  // Returns -1

Chapter 5: Generic Interfaces

5.1 Defining Generic Interfaces

Interfaces can be parameterized just like classes:

public interface IRepository<TEntity> where TEntity : class
{
    TEntity GetById(int id);
    IEnumerable<TEntity> GetAll();
    void Add(TEntity entity);
    void Update(TEntity entity);
    void Delete(TEntity entity);
}

5.2 Implementing Generic Interfaces

public class EmployeeRepository : IRepository<Employee>
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;
    
    public EmployeeRepository(AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }
    
    public Employee GetById(int id) => _context.Employees.Find(id);
    public IEnumerable<Employee> GetAll() => _context.Employees.ToList();
    public void Add(Employee entity) => _context.Employees.Add(entity);
    public void Update(Employee entity) => _context.Employees.Update(entity);
    public void Delete(Employee entity) => _context.Employees.Remove(entity);
}

5.3 Key Generic Interfaces in .NET

The .NET Base Class Library is rich with generic interfaces:

Interface Purpose
IEnumerable<T> Iteration over a sequence
ICollection<T> Sized, modifiable collection
IList<T> Indexed access
IDictionary<TKey, TValue> Key-value mapping
IComparable<T> Type-safe comparison
IEquatable<T> Type-safe equality
IComparer<T> External comparison logic
IEqualityComparer<T> External equality logic

Part IV: Constraints — Controlling Generic Flexibility

Chapter 6: The Need for Constraints

6.1 The Problem: Too Much Freedom

Consider this innocent-looking generic method:

public static T Max<T>(T a, T b)
{
    if (a > b)  // Compile error!
        return a;
    return b;
}

This won't compile. Why? The compiler knows nothing about T. It could be int, which supports >, or it could be Employee, which might not. Without knowing what operations T supports, the compiler must reject the code.

6.2 Constraints to the Rescue

Constraints tell the compiler: "I promise T will have certain capabilities."

public static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
{
    if (a.CompareTo(b) > 0)
        return a;
    return b;
}

Now the compiler knows T implements IComparable<T>, which guarantees the CompareTo method exists.

Chapter 7: Types of Constraints

7.1 Reference Type Constraint (class)

Restricts T to reference types (classes, interfaces, delegates, arrays):

public class EntityCache<T> where T : class
{
    private T _cached;
    
    public T GetOrDefault()
    {
        return _cached;  // Can be null
    }
}

7.2 Value Type Constraint (struct)

Restricts T to non-nullable value types:

public struct Nullable<T> where T : struct
{
    private readonly T _value;
    private readonly bool _hasValue;
    
    // This is essentially how System.Nullable<T> works
}

7.3 Constructor Constraint (new())

Requires T to have a public parameterless constructor:

public static T CreateInstance<T>() where T : new()
{
    return new T();  // Now this is valid!
}

// Usage
var employee = CreateInstance<Employee>();  // Works if Employee has parameterless ctor

7.4 Base Class Constraint

Restricts T to a specific class or its descendants:

public class AnimalShelter<T> where T : Animal
{
    private List<T> _animals = new List<T>();
    
    public void Admit(T animal)
    {
        animal.Feed();  // Valid: Animal has Feed() method
        _animals.Add(animal);
    }
}

// Usage
var dogShelter = new AnimalShelter<Dog>();  // Dog : Animal
var catShelter = new AnimalShelter<Cat>();  // Cat : Animal
// var carShelter = new AnimalShelter<Car>();  // Error: Car doesn't inherit Animal

7.5 Interface Constraint

Restricts T to types implementing specific interfaces:

public class SortedCollection<T> where T : IComparable<T>
{
    private List<T> _items = new List<T>();
    
    public void Add(T item)
    {
        int index = _items.BinarySearch(item);  // Uses IComparable<T>
        if (index < 0) index = ~index;
        _items.Insert(index, item);
    }
}

7.6 Multiple Constraints

Constraints can be combined:

public class Repository<TEntity> 
    where TEntity : class, IEntity, new()
{
    public TEntity Create()
    {
        var entity = new TEntity();  // new() constraint
        entity.Id = GenerateId();    // IEntity constraint
        return entity;               // class constraint allows null checks
    }
}

7.7 The notnull Constraint (C# 8.0+)

In nullable reference type contexts, ensures T cannot be null:

public class NonNullCache<T> where T : notnull
{
    private Dictionary<string, T> _cache = new();
    
    public void Set(string key, T value)
    {
        _cache[key] = value;  // value is guaranteed non-null
    }
}

7.8 The unmanaged Constraint (C# 7.3+)

Restricts to unmanaged types (primitives and structs containing only unmanaged types):

public unsafe void ProcessBuffer<T>(T* buffer, int length) where T : unmanaged
{
    // Can use pointer arithmetic with T
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++)
    {
        Process(buffer[i]);
    }
}

Chapter 8: Constraint Combinations and Rules

8.1 Constraint Ordering

When specifying multiple constraints, they must appear in a specific order:

  1. class or struct (mutually exclusive)
  2. Base class name (if any)
  3. Interface names
  4. new() (must be last)
// Correct order
public class Example<T> 
    where T : class, BaseClass, IInterface1, IInterface2, new()
{ }

8.2 Constraints on Multiple Type Parameters

Each type parameter can have its own constraints:

public class Mapper<TSource, TDestination>
    where TSource : class
    where TDestination : class, new()
{
    public TDestination Map(TSource source)
    {
        var destination = new TDestination();
        // Map properties...
        return destination;
    }
}

Part V: Advanced Topics

Chapter 9: Covariance and Contravariance

9.1 The Variance Problem

Consider this scenario:

class Animal { }
class Dog : Animal { }

List<Dog> dogs = new List<Dog>();
List<Animal> animals = dogs;  // Compile error! Why?

Intuitively, since every Dog is an Animal, a list of dogs should be usable as a list of animals. But consider:

animals.Add(new Cat());  // This would corrupt the dog list!

This is why List<T> doesn't allow such assignments. But sometimes variance is safe...

9.2 Covariance (out keyword)

Covariance allows a generic type to preserve the inheritance relationship of its type argument. It's safe when the type parameter is only used in output positions:

public interface IProducer<out T>
{
    T Produce();  // T only appears as output (return type)
}

class AnimalProducer : IProducer<Animal>
{
    public Animal Produce() => new Animal();
}

class DogProducer : IProducer<Dog>
{
    public Dog Produce() => new Dog();
}

// Now this is valid:
IProducer<Animal> producer = new DogProducer();
Animal animal = producer.Produce();  // Safe! We get a Dog, which is an Animal

IEnumerable<T> is covariant:

IEnumerable<Dog> dogs = new List<Dog>();
IEnumerable<Animal> animals = dogs;  // Valid! IEnumerable only produces items

9.3 Contravariance (in keyword)

Contravariance reverses the inheritance relationship. It's safe when the type parameter is only used in input positions:

public interface IConsumer<in T>
{
    void Consume(T item);  // T only appears as input (parameter)
}

class AnimalConsumer : IConsumer<Animal>
{
    public void Consume(Animal animal) => Console.WriteLine("Fed an animal");
}

// Now this is valid:
IConsumer<Dog> dogConsumer = new AnimalConsumer();
dogConsumer.Consume(new Dog());  // Safe! AnimalConsumer can handle any Animal

Action<T> and IComparer<T> are contravariant:

Action<Animal> feedAnimal = a => Console.WriteLine($"Feeding {a}");
Action<Dog> feedDog = feedAnimal;  // Valid! Something that handles Animals can handle Dogs
feedDog(new Dog());

9.4 Invariance

When a type parameter appears in both input and output positions, variance is not possible:

public interface ITransformer<T>
{
    T Transform(T input);  // T is both input and output
}
// ITransformer<T> is invariant

Chapter 10: Static Members in Generic Types

10.1 Static Fields Are Per Constructed Type

A critical detail often overlooked:

public class Counter<T>
{
    public static int Count = 0;
    
    public Counter()
    {
        Count++;
    }
}

// Usage
var intCounter1 = new Counter<int>();
var intCounter2 = new Counter<int>();
var stringCounter = new Counter<string>();

Console.WriteLine(Counter<int>.Count);     // 2
Console.WriteLine(Counter<string>.Count);  // 1

Each constructed type (Counter<int>, Counter<string>) has its own static field. They are completely independent.

10.2 Static Constructors

Static constructors also run once per constructed type:

public class TypeLogger<T>
{
    static TypeLogger()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"TypeLogger<{typeof(T).Name}> initialized");
    }
}

// Using TypeLogger<int> and TypeLogger<string> prints two messages

Chapter 11: Generic Type Inference

11.1 How Inference Works

The compiler examines method arguments to infer type parameters:

public static List<T> CreateList<T>(T first, T second)
{
    return new List<T> { first, second };
}

// Compiler infers T from arguments
var ints = CreateList(1, 2);           // List<int>
var strings = CreateList("a", "b");    // List<string>

11.2 Inference Limitations

Inference only works from arguments, not return types:

public static T Parse<T>(string value) { /* ... */ }

// This won't work:
int number = Parse("42");  // Error: Cannot infer T

// You must specify:
int number = Parse<int>("42");

11.3 Complex Inference

The compiler can infer through multiple levels:

public static TResult Select<TSource, TResult>(
    TSource source, 
    Func<TSource, TResult> selector)
{
    return selector(source);
}

// Both TSource and TResult are inferred
string result = Select(42, n => n.ToString());  
// TSource = int, TResult = string

Chapter 12: Reflection and Generics

12.1 Examining Generic Types at Runtime

Type listType = typeof(List<int>);

Console.WriteLine(listType.IsGenericType);           // True
Console.WriteLine(listType.IsConstructedGenericType); // True

Type[] args = listType.GetGenericArguments();
Console.WriteLine(args[0]);  // System.Int32

Type definition = listType.GetGenericTypeDefinition();
Console.WriteLine(definition);  // System.Collections.Generic.List`1[T]

12.2 Open vs. Closed Generic Types

Type openType = typeof(Dictionary<,>);   // Open: no type arguments
Type closedType = typeof(Dictionary<string, int>);  // Closed: fully specified

Console.WriteLine(openType.IsGenericTypeDefinition);    // True
Console.WriteLine(closedType.IsGenericTypeDefinition);  // False

12.3 Creating Generic Types Dynamically

Type openList = typeof(List<>);
Type closedList = openList.MakeGenericType(typeof(string));
object instance = Activator.CreateInstance(closedList);

// instance is now a List<string>
var list = (List<string>)instance;
list.Add("Dynamic!");

12.4 Invoking Generic Methods via Reflection

public class Processor
{
    public void Process<T>(T item)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Processing {typeof(T).Name}: {item}");
    }
}

// Invoke via reflection
var processor = new Processor();
MethodInfo openMethod = typeof(Processor).GetMethod("Process");
MethodInfo closedMethod = openMethod.MakeGenericMethod(typeof(int));
closedMethod.Invoke(processor, new object[] { 42 });

Part VI: Patterns and Best Practices

Chapter 13: Common Generic Patterns

13.1 The Repository Pattern

public interface IRepository<TEntity> where TEntity : class, IEntity
{
    Task<TEntity?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<TEntity>> GetAllAsync();
    Task<TEntity> AddAsync(TEntity entity);
    Task UpdateAsync(TEntity entity);
    Task DeleteAsync(TEntity entity);
}

public class Repository<TEntity> : IRepository<TEntity> 
    where TEntity : class, IEntity
{
    protected readonly DbContext _context;
    protected readonly DbSet<TEntity> _dbSet;
    
    public Repository(DbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
        _dbSet = context.Set<TEntity>();
    }
    
    public virtual async Task<TEntity?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
    {
        return await _dbSet.FindAsync(id);
    }
    
    public virtual async Task<IReadOnlyList<TEntity>> GetAllAsync()
    {
        return await _dbSet.ToListAsync();
    }
    
    // ... other implementations
}

13.2 The Factory Pattern

public interface IFactory<out T>
{
    T Create();
}

public class ServiceFactory<T> : IFactory<T> where T : class, new()
{
    public T Create() => new T();
}

// With parameters using Func<T>
public class ConfigurableFactory<T>
{
    private readonly Func<T> _creator;
    
    public ConfigurableFactory(Func<T> creator)
    {
        _creator = creator;
    }
    
    public T Create() => _creator();
}

13.3 The Specification Pattern

public interface ISpecification<T>
{
    bool IsSatisfiedBy(T entity);
    Expression<Func<T, bool>> ToExpression();
}

public abstract class Specification<T> : ISpecification<T>
{
    public bool IsSatisfiedBy(T entity)
    {
        return ToExpression().Compile()(entity);
    }
    
    public abstract Expression<Func<T, bool>> ToExpression();
    
    public Specification<T> And(Specification<T> other)
    {
        return new AndSpecification<T>(this, other);
    }
    
    public Specification<T> Or(Specification<T> other)
    {
        return new OrSpecification<T>(this, other);
    }
}

// Usage
public class ActiveEmployeeSpecification : Specification<Employee>
{
    public override Expression<Func<Employee, bool>> ToExpression()
    {
        return e => e.IsActive && e.TerminationDate == null;
    }
}

13.4 The Result/Either Pattern

public class Result<TSuccess, TFailure>
{
    public TSuccess? Success { get; }
    public TFailure? Failure { get; }
    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    
    private Result(TSuccess success)
    {
        Success = success;
        IsSuccess = true;
    }
    
    private Result(TFailure failure)
    {
        Failure = failure;
        IsSuccess = false;
    }
    
    public static Result<TSuccess, TFailure> Ok(TSuccess value) => new(value);
    public static Result<TSuccess, TFailure> Fail(TFailure error) => new(error);
    
    public TResult Match<TResult>(
        Func<TSuccess, TResult> onSuccess,
        Func<TFailure, TResult> onFailure)
    {
        return IsSuccess ? onSuccess(Success!) : onFailure(Failure!);
    }
}

// Usage
public Result<Employee, string> CreateEmployee(string name, string email)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(name))
        return Result<Employee, string>.Fail("Name is required");
    
    if (!IsValidEmail(email))
        return Result<Employee, string>.Fail("Invalid email format");
    
    var employee = new Employee { Name = name, Email = email };
    return Result<Employee, string>.Ok(employee);
}

// Consuming
var result = CreateEmployee("Alice", "alice@example.com");
var message = result.Match(
    onSuccess: emp => $"Created employee: {emp.Name}",
    onFailure: err => $"Error: {err}"
);

Chapter 14: Best Practices

14.1 Naming Conventions

  • Single type parameter: T
  • Multiple parameters: Descriptive names starting with T
// Good
Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
Func<TInput, TOutput>
IRepository<TEntity>

// Avoid
Dictionary<K, V>  // Not immediately clear
List<Type>        // Confusing with System.Type

14.2 Prefer Generic Collections

Always prefer System.Collections.Generic over System.Collections:

// Good
List<Employee> employees = new();
Dictionary<string, int> scores = new();

// Avoid
ArrayList employees = new();  // Boxing, no type safety
Hashtable scores = new();     // Boxing, no type safety

14.3 Use Constraints Judiciously

Add constraints only when necessary:

// Over-constrained: Do we really need all these?
public class Repository<T> 
    where T : class, IEntity, IValidatable, IAuditable, new()

// Better: Only what's actually used
public class Repository<T> where T : class, IEntity

14.4 Consider Variance When Designing Interfaces

If your interface only produces T, make it covariant:

public interface IReadOnlyRepository<out TEntity>
{
    TEntity GetById(int id);
    IEnumerable<TEntity> GetAll();
}

If it only consumes T, make it contravariant:

public interface IValidator<in T>
{
    bool Validate(T item);
}

14.5 Avoid Excessive Generic Nesting

// Hard to read
Dictionary<string, List<Tuple<int, Dictionary<string, object>>>> data;

// Better: Create meaningful types
class UserData { /* ... */ }
Dictionary<string, UserData> data;

Part VII: Generics in the .NET Ecosystem

Chapter 15: Generics in Entity Framework Core

15.1 DbSet<T>

public class AppDbContext : DbContext
{
    public DbSet<Employee> Employees { get; set; }
    public DbSet<Department> Departments { get; set; }
}

// DbSet<T> provides generic query and change tracking
var employees = await context.Employees
    .Where(e => e.IsActive)
    .ToListAsync();

15.2 Generic Configuration

public abstract class BaseEntityConfiguration<T> : IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>
    where T : BaseEntity
{
    public virtual void Configure(EntityTypeBuilder<T> builder)
    {
        builder.HasKey(e => e.Id);
        builder.Property(e => e.CreatedAt).IsRequired();
        builder.Property(e => e.UpdatedAt).IsRequired();
    }
}

public class EmployeeConfiguration : BaseEntityConfiguration<Employee>
{
    public override void Configure(EntityTypeBuilder<Employee> builder)
    {
        base.Configure(builder);
        builder.Property(e => e.Name).HasMaxLength(100);
    }
}

Chapter 16: Generics in Dependency Injection

16.1 Generic Service Registration

// Register open generic
services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(Repository<>));

// Now any IRepository<T> resolves to Repository<T>
// IRepository<Employee> → Repository<Employee>
// IRepository<Product> → Repository<Product>

16.2 Generic Decorators

public class CachingRepository<T> : IRepository<T> where T : class, IEntity
{
    private readonly IRepository<T> _inner;
    private readonly IMemoryCache _cache;
    
    public CachingRepository(IRepository<T> inner, IMemoryCache cache)
    {
        _inner = inner;
        _cache = cache;
    }
    
    public async Task<T?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
    {
        string key = $"{typeof(T).Name}_{id}";
        return await _cache.GetOrCreateAsync(key, 
            entry => _inner.GetByIdAsync(id));
    }
}

// Registration with decoration (using Scrutor)
services.Decorate(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(CachingRepository<>));

Chapter 17: Generics in Blazor

17.1 Generic Components

@typeparam TItem

<ul>
    @foreach (var item in Items)
    {
        <li>@ItemTemplate(item)</li>
    }
</ul>

@code {
    [Parameter] public IEnumerable<TItem> Items { get; set; } = default!;
    [Parameter] public RenderFragment<TItem> ItemTemplate { get; set; } = default!;
}

Usage:

<GenericList Items="employees" Context="emp">
    <ItemTemplate>
        <span>@emp.Name - @emp.Department</span>
    </ItemTemplate>
</GenericList>

17.2 Generic Component Constraints

@typeparam TEntity where TEntity : IEntity

<MudTable Items="@Items" Hover="true">
    <HeaderContent>
        <MudTh>ID</MudTh>
        <MudTh>Actions</MudTh>
    </HeaderContent>
    <RowTemplate>
        <MudTd>@context.Id</MudTd>  @* IEntity guarantees Id exists *@
        <MudTd>
            <MudIconButton Icon="@Icons.Material.Filled.Edit" 
                          OnClick="() => Edit(context)" />
        </MudTd>
    </RowTemplate>
</MudTable>

@code {
    [Parameter] public IEnumerable<TEntity> Items { get; set; } = default!;
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<TEntity> OnEdit { get; set; }
    
    private async Task Edit(TEntity entity) => await OnEdit.InvokeAsync(entity);
}

Appendix A: Quick Reference

Constraint Syntax Summary

Constraint Meaning
where T : class T must be a reference type
where T : struct T must be a non-nullable value type
where T : new() T must have a parameterless constructor
where T : BaseClass T must inherit from BaseClass
where T : IInterface T must implement IInterface
where T : notnull T must be non-nullable (C# 8+)
where T : unmanaged T must be an unmanaged type (C# 7.3+)
where T : U T must derive from type parameter U

Variance Summary

Keyword Name Direction Safe When
out Covariance Child → Parent T is only returned
in Contravariance Parent → Child T is only accepted
(none) Invariance No conversion T is both input and output

Appendix B: Further Reading

  1. C# Language Specification — The official reference for generic syntax and semantics
  2. "CLR via C#" by Jeffrey Richter — Deep dive into how generics work at the runtime level
  3. "C# in Depth" by Jon Skeet — Excellent coverage of generic evolution across C# versions
  4. Microsoft Docs: Generic Classes — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/
  5. Entity Framework Core Documentation — Practical examples of generics in ORM contexts

This guide was written as an educational resource for .NET developers seeking to master generics. Understanding generics deeply will improve your ability to write reusable, type-safe, and performant code.

topics.title: Delegates, Lambdas & Expression Bodies
topics.contentHtml:
Delegates, Lambdas &
Expression-Bodied Members

A "for dummies" deep dive into three C# concepts that share an arrow

Table of Contents

  1. Part 1: Delegates — "A Variable That Holds a Method"
  2. Part 2: Lambdas — "A Method Without a Name"
  3. Part 3: Expression-Bodied Members — "Just Shorthand"
  4. Part 4: The Big Comparison — Telling Them Apart
  5. Part 5: Practice Exercises

Part 1: Delegates

"A variable that holds a method"

Think of a delegate like a job posting.

A job posting says: "I need someone who can take a string and return a number." It doesn't say who will do the job — it just describes the shape of the work (what goes in, what comes out).

When you assign a method to a delegate, you're hiring someone for that job. The posting (delegate type) stays the same; you're just filling the position.

The Basics

Normally, when you call a method, you know exactly which method you're calling:

int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;

var result = Add(3, 4);  // You KNOW you're calling Add

But what if you want to say: "I'll call some method that takes two ints and returns an int — but I don't know which one yet"?

That's what a delegate does. It's a typed container for a method reference.

// Step 1: Declare the "job posting" (the delegate type)
delegate int MathOperation(int a, int b);

// Step 2: Create real methods that match the posting
int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;
int Multiply(int a, int b) => a * b;

// Step 3: "Hire" a method for the job
MathOperation operation = Add;       // operation now "points to" Add

var result = operation(3, 4);       // calls Add(3, 4) → returns 7

// Step 4: You can swap who does the job!
operation = Multiply;               // now it points to Multiply
result = operation(3, 4);           // calls Multiply(3, 4) → returns 12

delegate int MathOperation(int a, int b);

"A MathOperation is any method that takes two ints and returns an int."


MathOperation operation = Add;

"Create a variable called operation and point it at the Add method."


operation(3, 4);

"Call whatever method operation is currently pointing to, with arguments 3 and 4."

Why Would I Ever Need This?

Delegates let you pass behavior as a parameter. Instead of passing data (numbers, strings), you pass actions.

// A method that applies ANY operation to two numbers
int Calculate(int a, int b, MathOperation whatToDo)
{
    return whatToDo(a, b);
}

// Now you can pass different behaviors:
Calculate(3, 4, Add);        // → 7   (passed Add as behavior)
Calculate(3, 4, Multiply);   // → 12  (passed Multiply as behavior)

Calculate(3, 4, Add)

"Calculate 3 and 4, and the way I want you to do it is by adding."


Calculate(3, 4, Multiply)

"Calculate 3 and 4, and the way I want you to do it is by multiplying."

Built-in Delegates: Func, Action, Predicate

Declaring your own delegate type every time is tedious. C# provides built-in ones:

Func<...>

Has a return value.
Last type parameter is the return type.

// Takes two ints, returns an int
Func<int, int, int> add = Add;
//    ↑in   ↑in   ↑out

// Takes a string, returns a bool
Func<string, bool> check = IsValid;
//    ↑in      ↑out

// Takes nothing, returns a string
Func<string> greet = SayHello;
//    ↑out (only one = return type)

Action<...>

No return value (void).
All type parameters are inputs.

// Takes a string, returns nothing
Action<string> log = Console.WriteLine;
//      ↑in

// Takes nothing, returns nothing
Action doStuff = CleanUp;
// (no type params at all)

log("hello");     // prints "hello"
doStuff();         // runs CleanUp()

Func<string, int> getLength = s => s.Length;

"getLength is a function that takes a string and returns an int."


Action<string> print = s => Console.WriteLine(s);

"print is an action that takes a string and does something with it (no return value)."

Delegate = a typed variable that holds a reference to a method. Think of it as: "I don't know WHICH method yet, but I know its SHAPE."

Use Func<...> when the method returns something. Use Action<...> when it returns void.

Part 2: Lambdas

"A method without a name"

If a delegate is a job posting, a lambda is a freelancer who shows up without a resume.

Instead of writing a full method, giving it a name, and then pointing a delegate to it, you just write the code right there, inline. It's a method that exists only where it's needed.

Like telling a taxi driver: "Turn left, then right, then stop" — you didn't name the route, you just described it on the spot.

The Evolution (How We Got Here)

Let's filter a list of numbers to keep only the even ones. Watch how the same logic gets shorter over C#'s history:

C# 1.0 — Named Method
// Step 1: Write a named method somewhere in your class
bool IsEven(int n)
{
    return n % 2 == 0;
}

// Step 2: Pass its name
var evens = numbers.Where(IsEven);
C# 2.0 — Anonymous Method (delegate keyword)
var evens = numbers.Where(
    delegate(int n) { return n % 2 == 0; }
);
C# 3.0 — Lambda Expression (what we use today)
var evens = numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0);

All three do exactly the same thing. The lambda is just the most concise way to write it.

Lambda Syntax Breakdown

n => n % 2 == 0 ↑ ↑ ↑ parameter "goes to" body (what to do)

n => n % 2 == 0

"Given n, check if n mod 2 equals 0."

Or even simpler: "n goes to n is even."

Reading Lambdas Like English

Here's a cheat sheet for reading the => in a lambda. Read it as "goes to" or "becomes" or "maps to":

// "x goes to x times 2"
x => x * 2

// "name goes to name starts with A"
name => name.StartsWith("A")

// "person goes to person's Age is greater than 18"
person => person.Age > 18

// "(a, b) goes to a plus b"
(a, b) => a + b

// "no input goes to 42"
() => 42

// With a body block (for multiple statements):
// "x goes to: do some stuff, then return the result"
x => {
    var doubled = x * 2;
    var plusOne = doubled + 1;
    return plusOne;
}

Lambdas in Real Life: LINQ

This is where you see lambdas 90% of the time. Every LINQ method takes a lambda that describes what to do with each element:

var people = new List<Person> { ... };

// "WHERE does the person's Age go to being greater than 18?"
// → In English: "Where the person's age is greater than 18"
people.Where(p => p.Age > 18)

// "SELECT: person goes to person's Name"
// → In English: "Select each person's name"
people.Select(p => p.Name)

// "ORDER BY: person goes to person's Age"
// → In English: "Order by each person's age"
people.OrderBy(p => p.Age)

// "ANY: person goes to person's Name equals John"
// → In English: "Is there any person whose name is John?"
people.Any(p => p.Name == "John")

// "FIRST: person goes to person's Name equals John"
// → In English: "Find the first person whose name is John"
people.First(p => p.Name == "John")

A Lambda IS a Delegate Value

This is the critical connection. A lambda is just a convenient way to create a delegate instance:

// These two are equivalent:

// 1. Named method + assign to delegate
bool IsEven(int n) { return n % 2 == 0; }
Func<int, bool> check = IsEven;

// 2. Lambda (anonymous method assigned to delegate in one step)
Func<int, bool> check = n => n % 2 == 0;

// Both produce the SAME result: a Func<int, bool> that checks evenness.
// The lambda just skips the "name it, then reference it" step.

Lambda = an anonymous (unnamed) function that creates a delegate value on the spot.

Read => as "goes to". The left side is input, the right side is what to do with it.

A lambda is literally filling a delegate's "job posting" with an unnamed freelancer.

Part 3: Expression-Bodied Members

"Just shorthand for a method/property body"

If a lambda is a freelancer, an expression-bodied member is a full-time employee with a very short job description.

It has a name, it lives in a class, it's a proper member — it's just that its body is so simple you can write it in one line with => instead of using curly braces and return.

It's cosmetic surgery on syntax, nothing more. The compiled result is identical.

The Core Idea

When a method or property body is a single expression, you can replace { return ...; } with => ...;

Traditional Body

public int Area()
{
    return Width * Height;
}

public string Name
{
    get { return _name; }
}

Expression Body

public int Area() => Width * Height;


public string Name => _name;

That's it. There's no deeper concept. It's literally just a shorter way to write { return ...; }.

Reading Expression-Bodied Members Like English

Read the => as "returns" or "is defined as" (NOT as "goes to"):

// "Name is defined as 'Builder'"
public string Name => "Builder";

// "Category is defined as 'Creational'"
public string Category => "Creational";

// "Area returns Width times Height"
public int Area() => Width * Height;

// "ToString returns a formatted string with Name and Text"
public override string ToString() => $"Element: {Name}, Text: {Text}";

Where Can You Use It?

Expression bodies work on almost any class member:

public class Demo
{
    private string _name;

    // Read-only property
    public string Name => _name;

    // Property with getter and setter
    public string Label
    {
        get => _name;
        set => _name = value;
    }

    // Method
    public int Double(int x) => x * 2;

    // Constructor
    public Demo(string name) => _name = name;

    // Void method (no return, just an expression)
    public void Log(string msg) => Console.WriteLine(msg);
}

From YOUR Codebase

// In BuilderDemo.cs — these are all expression-bodied PROPERTIES:
public string Name => "Builder";        // "Name is defined as 'Builder'"
public string Category => "Creational"; // "Category is defined as 'Creational'"
public int Order => 1;                  // "Order is defined as 1"

// These are NOT lambdas. They're getter-only properties.
// Equivalent to:
public string Name { get { return "Builder"; } }

Expression-bodied member = shorthand for writing a single-expression method/property body.

Read => as "returns" or "is defined as".

It has a name. It lives in a class. It's NOT a lambda. It's just shorter syntax.

Part 4: The Big Comparison

They both use =>, but they're completely different things.

The => arrow is used in two unrelated contexts in C#. This is the #1 source of confusion. The arrow itself means nothing on its own — its meaning depends entirely on where it appears.

Where does the => appear?

  • On a class member declaration (after a method name, property name, etc.) → It's an expression-bodied member
  • Everywhere else (assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, inside LINQ) → It's a lambda

Side by Side

public class Example
{
    // ═══ EXPRESSION-BODIED MEMBERS ═══
    // These have names. They live in a class. They ARE the member.

    public int Double(int x) => x * 2;       // Named method. NOT a lambda.
    public string Name => "Hello";            // Named property. NOT a lambda.


    // ═══ LAMBDAS ═══
    // These are VALUES — anonymous functions used where a value is expected.

    public void Demo()
    {
        // Stored in a variable (Func is a delegate type)
        Func<int, int> doubler = x => x * 2;    // Lambda! (assigned to a variable)

        // Passed as an argument
        var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
        list.Select(x => x * 2);                // Lambda! (passed to a method)
        list.Where(x => x > 1);                 // Lambda! (passed to a method)
    }
}

The Visual Test

Does the => have a CLASS MEMBER to the left? (a method name, property name, constructor, etc.) ┌──── YES ────┐ │ │ ▼ │ Expression-bodied │ member │ │ ┌──── NO ────┘ │ ▼ Lambda

What They Compile To

// Expression-bodied method
public int Double(int x) => x * 2;
// Compiles to a regular method:
// public int Double(int x) { return x * 2; }
// Nothing special. Just a normal method with shorter syntax.

// Lambda
Func<int, int> doubler = x => x * 2;
// Compiles to a delegate OBJECT:
// The compiler creates a hidden method AND a delegate instance pointing to it.
// It's a thing you can store, pass around, and invoke later.
Expression-bodied = how you write a member (syntax)
Lambda = a value you create (a function object)

Part 5: Practice Exercises

Exercise 1: Identify the Arrow

For each line, is the => an expression-bodied member or a lambda?

a) public string FullName => $"{First} {Last}";
b) names.Where(n => n.Length > 3);
c) public void Greet() => Console.WriteLine("Hi");
d) Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;
e) public int Order => 5;
Show Answers

a) Expression-bodied — it's a property (class member on the left)
b) Lambda — passed as an argument to Where
c) Expression-bodied — it's a void method (class member on the left)
d) Lambda — assigned to a Func variable
e) Expression-bodied — it's a property (class member on the left)

Exercise 2: Read Like English

Translate each line to plain English:

a) products.Where(p => p.Price > 100)
b) public string Category => "SOLID";
c) people.Select(p => p.Name)
d) Action<string> yell = s => Console.WriteLine(s.ToUpper());
Show Answers

a) "From products, keep only those where the product's price is greater than 100."
b) "The Category property is defined as 'SOLID'."
c) "From people, select each person's name."
d) "yell is an action that takes a string and writes it to the console in uppercase."

Exercise 3: Delegate Understanding

What does this code print?

Func<int, int, int> operation = (a, b) => a + b;
Console.WriteLine(operation(3, 4));

operation = (a, b) => a * b;
Console.WriteLine(operation(3, 4));
Show Answer

Prints 7 then 12.
First, operation points to an "add" lambda, so 3+4=7.
Then it's reassigned to a "multiply" lambda, so 3*4=12.
The delegate variable changed what method it points to.

Exercise 4: Convert Between Styles

Rewrite this expression-bodied property as a traditional property with { get { } }:

public string Greeting => $"Hello, {Name}";
Show Answer 
public string Greeting
{
    get
    {
        return $"Hello, {Name}";
    }
}

They compile to the exact same thing. The expression-bodied version is just shorter.

Quick Reference Card

delegate = a type that describes a method's shape
Func<in, out> = built-in delegate (has return value)
Action<in> = built-in delegate (void)
x => x + 1 (in a value position) = lambda (creates a delegate)
int Foo() => x + 1; (on a member) = expression-bodied (just shorter syntax)

topics.title: Generics & Builders Deep Dive
topics.contentHtml:
Generics, Builders &
Everything In Between

From Class<T> to Functional Builders — a complete walkthrough using your codebase

Table of Contents

  1. Part 1: Generics — "A Class with a Blank"
  2. Part 2: Constraints — "Not Just Any Blank"
  3. Part 3: Recursive Generics — "Tell Me Who You Are"
  4. Part 4: Returning Interfaces — "You Can Only See This Much"
  5. Part 5: Extension Methods — "Adding Methods From Outside"
  6. Part 6: Delegates as Data — "Storing Behavior in a List"
  7. Part 7: The Functional Builder — "Putting It All Together"
  8. Part 8: Aggregate — "The Assembly Line"
  9. Part 9: Practice Exercises

Part 1: Generics

"A class with a blank to fill in later"

Think of a generic class like a form with a blank field.

A Box<T> is like a shipping label that says: "Contents: ________". When you create Box<int>, you fill in the blank with "int". The box doesn't care what's inside — it just needs to know so it can handle it properly.

The Simplest Generic

public class Box<T>
{
    public T Content { get; set; }
}

T is not a real type. It's a placeholder that becomes real when you use the class:

var intBox = new Box<int>();          // T = int    → Content is an int
var strBox = new Box<string>();       // T = string → Content is a string
var pBox   = new Box<Person>();       // T = Person → Content is a Person

Box<T> → "A Box that holds something, and that something is called T."

Box<int> → "A Box where T is int."

Box<Person> → "A Box where T is Person."

You Already Use This Every Day

List<int>                // "A list where T is int"
List<string>             // "A list where T is string"
List<HtmlElement>        // "A list where T is HtmlElement"
HashSet<(Person, Relationship, Person)>  // "A hashset where T is that tuple"

List<T> is just a class that said: "I'm a list, but I don't know what I hold yet — you tell me."

Multiple Type Parameters

A class can have more than one blank:

public class Pair<TFirst, TSecond>
{
    public TFirst First { get; set; }
    public TSecond Second { get; set; }
}

var pair = new Pair<string, int>();   // First is string, Second is int
pair.First = "age";
pair.Second = 25;

Pair<string, int> → "A Pair where the first thing is a string and the second thing is an int."

Why Not Just Use object?

Without Generics (object)

public class Box
{
    public object Content { get; set; }
}

var box = new Box();
box.Content = 42;

// Have to cast — could crash at runtime!
string s = (string)box.Content; // BOOM

With Generics

public class Box<T>
{
    public T Content { get; set; }
}

var box = new Box<int>();
box.Content = 42;

// Compiler stops you BEFORE running
string s = box.Content; // Compile error!

Generics give you: write once, fully type-safe. No casting, no runtime crashes.

Generic = a class/method with a type placeholder (T) that gets filled in when you use it. It lets you write code once that works with many types, without losing compile-time safety.

Part 2: Constraints

"Not just any blank — I have requirements"

If a generic is a form with a blank, a constraint is the fine print next to the blank: "Must be at least 18 years old" or "Must have a valid ID."

It restricts what you're allowed to fill in.

The Syntax

public class Repo<T> where T : class
//                      ↑ "T must be a reference type (not int, bool, etc.)"

public class Sorter<T> where T : IComparable<T>
//                         ↑ "T must implement IComparable"

public class Zoo<T> where T : Animal
//                      ↑ "T must be Animal or a subclass of Animal"

public class Factory<T> where T : new()
//                          ↑ "T must have a parameterless constructor"

public class Wrapper<T> where T : struct
//                          ↑ "T must be a value type (int, bool, double, enums, custom structs)"

Reference Types vs Value Types

class and struct constraints are mutually exclusive — you pick one or neither:

ConstraintAllowsExamples
where T : classReference types onlystring, Person, List<int>, any class
where T : structValue types onlyint, bool, double, DateTime, enums, custom structs
public class RefOnly<T> where T : class { }
public class ValOnly<T> where T : struct { }

RefOnly<string> ok1;      // string is a reference type ✓
RefOnly<int> fail1;       // int is a value type ✗ COMPILE ERROR

ValOnly<int> ok2;         // int is a value type ✓
ValOnly<string> fail2;    // string is a reference type ✗ COMPILE ERROR

Note: The struct constraint also guarantees T is non-nullable — you can't pass int? (Nullable<int>). If you want to allow both reference and value types but require neither to be null, C# 8+ has where T : notnull.

where T : Animal → "T can be anything, as long as it's an Animal or a subclass of Animal."

where T : new() → "T must have a parameterless constructor, so I can do new T()."

Why Constraints Matter

Without constraints, the compiler only knows T is "some type" — it can't assume anything about what T can do:

public class Factory<T>
{
    public T Create()
    {
        return new T();  // ERROR! What if T doesn't have a constructor?
    }
}

// With the constraint, the compiler trusts you:
public class Factory<T> where T : new()
{
    public T Create()
    {
        return new T();  // OK! The constraint guarantees T has a constructor.
    }
}

In your FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>:

where TSubject : new() — this is why Build() can do new TSubject(). Without it, the compiler would say: "I don't know if TSubject has a parameterless constructor!"

Multiple Constraints

You can stack them, and you can constrain multiple type parameters:

public class FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>
    where TSelf : FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>   // constraint on TSelf
    where TSubject : new()                                // constraint on TSubject

Read it as: "TSelf must extend FunctionalBuilder, AND TSubject must have a parameterless constructor."

Constraint = a restriction on what types can fill in a generic parameter. It tells the compiler "T isn't just anything — it has these guarantees", which unlocks operations that need those guarantees (like new T()).

Part 3: Recursive Generics

"Tell me who you are, so I can return you"

Imagine a relay race. The baton-passing rule says: "When you hand off the baton, it must go back to the same team."

The parent class holds the baton (the return type). It says: "I'll pass the baton, but I need to know which team you're on." The child says: "I'm on team PersonJobBuilder." Now the parent can hand the baton back to the right team.

The Problem

In fluent builders, every method returns this so you can chain. But with inheritance, the parent returns itself, not the child:

public class PersonInfoBuilder
{
    public PersonInfoBuilder Called(string name) // returns PersonInfoBuilder
    {
        person.name = name;
        return this;
    }
}

public class PersonJobBuilder : PersonInfoBuilder
{
    public PersonJobBuilder WorksAsA(string position) { ... }
}

// THE PROBLEM:
new PersonJobBuilder()
    .Called("John")      // returns PersonInfoBuilder ← NOT PersonJobBuilder!
    .WorksAsA("dev")    // COMPILE ERROR! PersonInfoBuilder has no WorksAsA()

The Solution

public class PersonInfoBuilder<TSelf>
    where TSelf : PersonInfoBuilder<TSelf>
{
    public TSelf Called(string name)   // returns TSelf — whatever the child is!
    {
        person.name = name;
        return (TSelf)this;
    }
}

The child fills in the blank with itself:

public class PersonJobBuilder : PersonInfoBuilder<PersonJobBuilder>
//                                                    ↑ TSelf = me!

Now Called() returns PersonJobBuilder (because TSelf = PersonJobBuilder), and the chain works:

new PersonJobBuilder()
    .Called("John")      // TSelf = PersonJobBuilder → returns PersonJobBuilder!
    .WorksAsA("dev")    // Works! Still on PersonJobBuilder.
    .Build()
The pattern: class Child : Parent<Child> The child passes ITSELF as the type argument. The parent uses it as the return type. Parent says: "Whoever inherits me, tell me your type." Child says: "TSelf is me." Parent says: "Great, I'll return you."

The generic <TSelf> is NOT about "working with data of type TSelf." It's a trick to let the parent class return the child's type without knowing which child it is. It's purely about return types for fluent chaining.

Recursive generic = class Child : Parent<Child>. The child passes itself as the type argument so the parent can return the child's type. This keeps fluent method chains working across inheritance.

Part 4: Returning Interfaces

"You can only see this much"

Imagine a person who is simultaneously a driver, a mechanic, and a salesman. They're all the same person.

When you return them as IDriver, the caller can only ask them to drive. They can't ask about car repairs or prices — even though the person knows how to do those things. The interface acts as a mask that hides everything except one role.

The Core Idea

You can't instantiate an interface. But you CAN return an object that implements it. The return type just controls what the caller can see.

public interface ISpecifyCarType
{
    ISpecifyWheelSize OfType(CarType type);   // returns "something that can specify wheels"
}

public interface ISpecifyWheelSize
{
    IBuildCar WithWheels(int size);            // returns "something that can build"
}

public interface IBuildCar
{
    Car Build();                               // returns the finished car
}

Your CarBuilder.Impl class implements all three interfaces. But each method returns this typed as the next interface:

private class Impl : ISpecifyCarType, ISpecifyWheelSize, IBuildCar
{
    public ISpecifyWheelSize OfType(CarType type)
    {
        car.Type = type;
        return this;    // same object, but caller only sees ISpecifyWheelSize
    }
}

How It Enforces Order

CarBuilder.Create() → returns ISpecifyCarType You can ONLY call: .OfType() .OfType(CarType.Sedan) → returns ISpecifyWheelSize You can ONLY call: .WithWheels() .WithWheels(18) → returns IBuildCar You can ONLY call: .Build() .Build() → returns Car (done!)

Try calling them out of order:

CarBuilder.Create().Build();          // ERROR: ISpecifyCarType has no Build()
CarBuilder.Create().WithWheels(18);   // ERROR: ISpecifyCarType has no WithWheels()
What the object IS: What you can SEE at each step: ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Impl │ │ │ │ .OfType() │ ◄── ISpecifyCarType shows only this │ .WithWheels() │ ◄── ISpecifyWheelSize shows only this │ .Build() │ ◄── IBuildCar shows only this │ │ └─────────────────────┘ Same object, three different "masks." Each mask reveals only the next step.

Returning an interface = returning an object, but the caller only sees the methods defined on that interface. Use this to restrict what's available at each step. The object has all methods; the interface is a mask.

Part 5: Extension Methods

"Adding methods from outside a class"

Imagine a toolbox (a class). It's sealed shut — you can't put new tools inside. But you can attach a tool to the outside using a magnet. Anyone holding the toolbox can use it as if it were built in.

Extension methods are those magnetic tools.

The Syntax

public static class PersonBuilderExtensions
{
    public static PersonBuilder WithPosition(
        this PersonBuilder builder,   // ← "this" = extension method
        string position)
    {
        return builder.Do(p => p.position = position);
    }
}

The this before the first parameter is the magic word. It tells C#: "this method can be called AS IF it were a method on PersonBuilder."

Called as static method

PersonBuilderExtensions
    .WithPosition(builder, "dev");

Called as extension method

builder.WithPosition("dev");

// looks like it belongs to
// PersonBuilder, but it doesn't!

These two are identical. The compiler rewrites the second into the first.

Rules for Extension Methods

  • Must be in a static class
  • Must be a static method
  • First parameter must have this keyword
  • The type after this determines what type the method "attaches" to

Why This Matters for Builders

PersonBuilder is sealed — you can't inherit from it. Without extension methods, the only way to add new builder steps is to modify the class itself. Extensions let you add methods without touching the original:

// Anyone, anywhere, can write this:
public static PersonBuilder WithAge(this PersonBuilder builder, int age)
    => builder.Do(p => p.age = age);

// And now this works:
new PersonBuilder().Called("John").WithAge(30).Build();

LINQ works exactly this way!

.Where(), .Select(), .OrderBy(), .Aggregate() — none of these are on List<T>. They're all extension methods defined in System.Linq. That's why you need using System.Linq; — without it, the compiler can't find them.

Extension method = a static method with this on the first parameter, letting you call it like it's a member of that type. Adds functionality without modifying the original class.

Part 6: Delegates as Data

"Storing behavior in a list"

Think of a recipe book. Each page is an instruction: "chop onions", "add salt", "stir for 5 minutes."

The recipe book doesn't DO anything by itself. It just collects instructions. The cooking only happens when someone reads the book and follows each step.

A List<Func<Person, Person>> is that recipe book. Each function is a page. Build() is the cook.

Functions as Values

In C#, functions can be stored in variables, put in lists, and passed around:

// A single function stored in a variable
Func<int, int> doubler = x => x * 2;

// A LIST of functions!
var operations = new List<Func<int, int>>();
operations.Add(x => x * 2);    // add "double" to the list
operations.Add(x => x + 10);   // add "plus 10" to the list
operations.Add(x => x / 3);    // add "divide by 3" to the list

// Run them all on a value:
int result = 5;
foreach (var op in operations)
{
    result = op(result);   // 5 → 10 → 20 → 6
}

The Action → Func Wrapping

The builder stores Func<Person, Person> (takes a Person, returns a Person). But it's more convenient for callers to use Action<Person> (takes a Person, returns nothing). So the builder wraps each Action:

What the caller provides

Action<Person>

p => p.name = "John"
// sets name, returns NOTHING

What the list needs

Func<Person, Person>

p => { p.name = "John"; return p; }
// sets name, returns the person

The AddAction method bridges the gap:

private TSelf AddAction(Action<TSubject> action)
{
    actions.Add(s =>       // "given a subject s..."
    {
        action(s);       // "run the action on s" (e.g., set s.name = "John")
        return s;        // "hand s back" (so the next function gets it)
    });
    return (TSelf)this;
}

action(s) — "I can call action with s because action is an Action<Person> — a variable holding a method that takes a Person."

Calling a delegate is just like calling a method: action(s) = "run whatever method action is pointing to, and pass it s."

The Key Insight: Nothing Runs Yet

new PersonBuilder()
    .Called("John")          // adds a recipe: "set name to John"
    .WithPosition("dev")    // adds a recipe: "set position to dev"
    // At this point: NO Person exists. Just two recipes in a list.
    .Build();               // NOW a Person is created and recipes are executed.

Writing a lambda doesn't execute it. It's like writing a note: "when you get a package, open it." The note sits in a list until Build() actually hands out the package. .Called("John") writes the note. .Build() runs it.

Part 7: The Functional Builder

"Putting it all together"

Now let's see how all the pieces combine in your actual code:

The Generic Base Class

public abstract class FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>
    where TSelf : FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>   // recursive generic (Part 3)
    where TSubject : new()                                // constraint (Part 2)
{
    private readonly List<Func<TSubject, TSubject>> actions = [];  // delegates as data (Part 6)

    private TSelf AddAction(Action<TSubject> action)  // Action→Func wrapping (Part 6)
    {
        actions.Add(s => { action(s); return s; });
        return (TSelf)this;                              // returns child type (Part 3)
    }

    public TSelf Do(Action<TSubject> action) => AddAction(action);
    public TSubject Build() => actions.Aggregate(new TSubject(), (s, f) => f(s));  // Part 8
}
Type ParameterMeansFor PersonBuilderFor CarBuilder
TSubject"What am I building?"PersonCar
TSelf"What's the concrete builder?"PersonBuilderCarBuilder

The Concrete Builders

// PersonBuilder fills in both blanks:
public sealed class PersonBuilder
    : FunctionalBuilder<Person, PersonBuilder>
//                      ↑ TSubject    ↑ TSelf
{
    public PersonBuilder Called(string name)
        => Do(p => p.name = name);   // Do() is inherited from base class!
}

// CarBuilder fills in the SAME blanks, different types:
public class CarBuilder
    : FunctionalBuilder<Car, CarBuilder>
//                      ↑ TSubject  ↑ TSelf
{
    public CarBuilder WithMake(string make) => Do(c => c.Make = make);
    public CarBuilder WithModel(string model) => Do(c => c.Model = model);
}

What the Base Class Looks Like After Substitution

When PersonBuilder fills in the blanks, mentally replace every TSubject with Person and every TSelf with PersonBuilder:

// What PersonBuilder inherits (after mental substitution):

private readonly List<Func<Person, Person>> actions = [];
//                         ↑ TSubject = Person

private PersonBuilder AddAction(Action<Person> action)
//      ↑ TSelf = PersonBuilder              ↑ TSubject = Person

public PersonBuilder Do(Action<Person> action) ...
public Person Build() => actions.Aggregate(new Person(), ...);
//     ↑ TSubject = Person                     ↑ new() constraint allows this

Extensions Add Even More Methods

// Without modifying PersonBuilder or FunctionalBuilder:
public static PersonBuilder WithPosition(
    this PersonBuilder builder,     // extension method (Part 5)
    string position)
{
    return builder.Do(p => p.position = position);
}

The Full Chain

var person = new PersonBuilder()       // creates a builder with an empty actions list
    .Called("John Doe")               // adds recipe: "set name" (method on PersonBuilder)
    .Do(p => p.gender = "Masculine") // adds recipe: "set gender" (inherited from base)
    .WithPosition("Software Engineer") // adds recipe: "set position" (extension method)
    .Build();                          // creates Person, runs ALL recipes on it

The Functional Builder combines: generics (reusable base), recursive generics (fluent chaining), constraints (new()), delegates as data (actions list), and extension methods (add steps from outside).

Part 8: Aggregate

"The assembly line"

Imagine a factory assembly line. A blank car frame enters at one end. At station 1, someone adds the engine. At station 2, someone paints it. At station 3, someone adds wheels. The same car passes through every station, getting modified at each one, and comes out finished at the end.

Aggregate is that assembly line.

The Signature

actions.Aggregate(
    new TSubject(),        // seed: the starting value (blank car frame)
    (s, f) => f(s)          // for each action: apply it to s, result becomes new s
)
ParameterWhat it isIn your builder
seedThe starting valuenew Person() — a fresh, empty person
sThe accumulated result (carries forward)The Person being built up
fThe current item from the listOne function from the actions list
f(s)Apply the function to the resultRun the recipe on the person

Concrete Trace

For: .Called("John").Do(p => p.position = "dev").Build()

Start
s = new Person() — fresh, empty person
Step 1
f = p => { p.name = "John"; return p; }
s = f(s) → s.name is now "John"
Step 2
f = p => { p.position = "dev"; return p; }
s = f(s) → s.position is now "dev"
Result
s = Person { name: "John", position: "dev" }

Aggregate Without the Magic (Just a Loop)

If Aggregate feels too abstract, this is the exact same thing:

public TSubject Build()
{
    var s = new TSubject();           // the seed
    foreach (var f in actions)        // walk through each function
    {
        s = f(s);                     // apply it, carry result forward
    }
    return s;                          // return the finished product
}

// Aggregate is just this loop compressed into one line:
public TSubject Build() => actions.Aggregate(new TSubject(), (s, f) => f(s));

The Full Signature Explained

public static TAccumulate Aggregate<TSource, TAccumulate>(
    this IEnumerable<TSource> source,          // the list to walk through
    TAccumulate seed,                          // starting value
    Func<TAccumulate, TSource, TAccumulate> func  // how to combine
)
Type ParameterMeansIn your builderIn a simpler example
TSource Type of items in the list Func<Person, Person> string (list of words)
TAccumulate Type of the result being carried Person int (a running total)

They can be different types! The list can hold one type and accumulate into another:

var words = new List<string> { "hello", "world", "foo" };

// TSource = string (items in the list)
// TAccumulate = int (the thing we're building up)
int totalLength = words.Aggregate(
    0,                                   // seed: start at 0
    (count, word) => count + word.Length   // add each word's length
);
// Step 0: count = 0
// Step 1: count = 0 + 5 ("hello")  → 5
// Step 2: count = 5 + 5 ("world")  → 10
// Step 3: count = 10 + 3 ("foo")   → 13

Aggregate = walk a list, carry a value, combine them at each step. It's a loop in one line. The seed is the starting value, and the lambda says how to combine each list item with the running result.

Part 9: Practice Exercises

Exercise 1: Read the Generics

What are TSubject and TSelf in this declaration?

public class CarBuilder : FunctionalBuilder<Car, CarBuilder> { }
Show Answer

TSubject = Car (what we're building), TSelf = CarBuilder (the concrete builder type for fluent chaining). Every Do() call returns CarBuilder. Every Build() call returns Car.

Exercise 2: Trace the Aggregate

What does this return?

var nums = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4 };
var result = nums.Aggregate(10, (acc, n) => acc + n);
Show Answer

20. Trace: 10 → 10+1=11 → 11+2=13 → 13+3=16 → 16+4=20.
The seed is 10, then each number in the list is added to the running total.

Exercise 3: Extension Method

Write an extension method WithYear for CarBuilder that sets the car's year. (Don't look at your code!)

Show Answer 
public static CarBuilder WithYear(this CarBuilder builder, int year)
    => builder.Do(c => c.Year = year);

// Or with full body syntax:
public static CarBuilder WithYear(this CarBuilder builder, int year)
{
    return builder.Do(c => c.Year = year);
}

Exercise 4: Identify the Concepts

For each numbered comment, which concept from this guide is being used?

public abstract class FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>       // 1.
    where TSelf : FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>          // 2.
    where TSubject : new()                                       // 3.
{
    private readonly List<Func<TSubject, TSubject>> actions = []; // 4.
    public TSubject Build() =>
        actions.Aggregate(new TSubject(), (s,f) => f(s));        // 5.
}
Show Answers

1. Generics (Part 1) — two type parameters
2. Recursive generic / constraint (Parts 2 & 3) — TSelf must extend the builder itself
3. Constraint (Part 2) — TSubject must have a parameterless constructor
4. Delegates as data (Part 6) — storing functions in a list
5. Aggregate (Part 8) — assembly line that runs all functions on a new TSubject

Exercise 5: Why Does return (TSelf)this Work?
