In AddAction, why is the cast (TSelf)this safe and not dangerous?

Show Answer

Because of the constraint where TSelf : FunctionalBuilder<TSubject, TSelf>. TSelf must be a subclass of FunctionalBuilder. And when you instantiate new PersonBuilder(), this IS a PersonBuilder at runtime. The cast just tells the compiler what it already is. The constraint guarantees no invalid type can sneak in.

Quick Reference Card

Class<T> = class with a type placeholder, filled in later
where T : X = restrict what T can be
class Child : Parent<Child> = recursive generic, for fluent return types
IFoo Method() = returns an object, but caller only sees IFoo's methods
this Type param = extension method, adds methods from outside
List<Func<...>> = storing functions as data (recipe book)
.Aggregate(seed, (acc, item) => ...) = assembly line loop in one line

topics.title: C# Flags Enum
topics.contentHtml:
C# Flags Enum Guide

What is the [Flags] Attribute?

The [Flags] attribute allows an enum to represent multiple values simultaneously using bitwise operations. It's ideal for situations where an entity can have multiple characteristics at the same time.

Practical Example: Employee Warnings

[Flags]
public enum EmployeeWarning
{
    None = 0,                   // 00000000 (binary)
    GeoLockNoLocation = 1,      // 00000001
    JobBoundNoSchedule = 2,     // 00000010
    InvalidLocationCheckIn = 4, // 00000100
    PendingValidation = 8,      // 00001000
    CheckInsDisabled = 16,      // 00010000
    NoScheduleAssigned = 32,    // 00100000
    NoLocationAssigned = 64,    // 01000000
    NoConfiguration = 128       // 10000000
}

Golden Rule: Powers of 2

Each value MUST be a power of 2:

  • 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024...

This is because each value occupies a unique bit in the binary representation:

Value Binary Bit Position
1 0000 0001 0
2 0000 0010 1
4 0000 0100 2
8 0000 1000 3
16 0001 0000 4
32 0010 0000 5
64 0100 0000 6
128 1000 0000 7

Basic Operations

1. Add a Flag

Use the |= operator (bitwise OR):

var warnings = EmployeeWarning.None;

// Add NoConfiguration
warnings |= EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration;
// warnings = 128 (10000000)

// Add NoScheduleAssigned
warnings |= EmployeeWarning.NoScheduleAssigned;
// warnings = 160 (10100000) = 128 + 32

2. Check if a Flag is Set

Use .HasFlag():

if (warnings.HasFlag(EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration))
{
    // This flag is active!
}

// Alternative (more performant but less readable):
if ((warnings & EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration) != 0)
{
    // This flag is active!
}

3. Remove a Flag

Use &= ~ (AND with NOT):

// Remove NoConfiguration
warnings &= ~EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration;

4. Check if ANY Flag is Set

if (warnings != EmployeeWarning.None)
{
    // Has at least one flag active
}

5. Clear All Flags

warnings = EmployeeWarning.None;

Real-World Example: LiveInsightsService

var insight = new LiveEmployeeInsight();

// Check employee configuration
var config = employee.Configuration;

if (config == null)
{
    // Add warning: no configuration
    insight.Warnings |= EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration;
}
else
{
    // Check if JobBound but missing schedule
    if (config.IsJobBound && !hasAnyJobScheduleToday)
    {
        insight.Warnings |= EmployeeWarning.JobBoundNoSchedule;
    }

    // Check if GeoLock required but no location source
    if (config.RequiresGeolocation && !hasAnyLocationSource)
    {
        insight.Warnings |= EmployeeWarning.GeoLockNoLocation;
    }
}

// At the end, the employee can have MULTIPLE warnings:
// warnings = GeoLockNoLocation | NoScheduleAssigned = 1 + 32 = 33

Usage in Blazor/Razor

@if (emp.HasWarnings)
{
    <div class="d-flex gap-1">
        @if (emp.Warnings.HasFlag(EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration))
        {
            <MudTooltip Text="No HR configuration found!">
                <MudIcon Icon="@Icons.Material.Filled.Settings" Color="Color.Error" />
            </MudTooltip>
        }
        @if (emp.Warnings.HasFlag(EmployeeWarning.JobBoundNoSchedule))
        {
            <MudTooltip Text="JobBound but no schedule assigned">
                <MudIcon Icon="@Icons.Material.Filled.EventBusy" Color="Color.Warning" />
            </MudTooltip>
        }
        @* ... more flags ... *@
    </div>
}

Pre-defined Combinations

You can define common combinations:

[Flags]
public enum EmployeeWarning
{
    None = 0,
    GeoLockNoLocation = 1,
    JobBoundNoSchedule = 2,
    InvalidLocationCheckIn = 4,

    // Combination: all urgent warnings
    AllUrgent = GeoLockNoLocation | JobBoundNoSchedule,  // = 3

    // Combination: all configuration issues
    AllConfigIssues = GeoLockNoLocation | JobBoundNoSchedule | InvalidLocationCheckIn  // = 7
}

Common Mistakes

❌ Using Values That Are NOT Powers of 2

// WRONG!
[Flags]
public enum BadExample
{
    None = 0,
    First = 1,
    Second = 2,
    Third = 3,  // ❌ 3 = 1 + 2, will conflict!
    Fourth = 4
}

❌ Forgetting the 0 Value (None)

// WRONG!
[Flags]
public enum BadExample
{
    First = 1,
    Second = 2
    // Without None = 0, there's no way to represent "nothing"
}

❌ Using == Instead of HasFlag

var warnings = EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration | EmployeeWarning.NoScheduleAssigned;

// WRONG - only true if warnings is EXACTLY NoConfiguration
if (warnings == EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration) { } // false!

// CORRECT - checks if NoConfiguration is included
if (warnings.HasFlag(EmployeeWarning.NoConfiguration)) { } // true!

Quick Reference

Operation Code Description
Add `flags \ = Flag` Bitwise OR
Remove flags &= ~Flag AND with NOT
Check flags.HasFlag(Flag) Returns bool
Clear All flags = None Full reset
Has Any? flags != None Any flag active

When to Use [Flags]?

✅ Use when:

  • An entity can have multiple simultaneous characteristics
  • You need to filter by combinations of characteristics
  • You want to represent permissions, states, or warnings

❌ Don't use when:

  • Values are mutually exclusive (use regular enum)
  • You need more than ~32 different values (use a different approach)
  • Logic is too complex (consider using classes instead)

Created for HRModule project - See EmployeeWarning in Services/Attendance/AttendanceModels.cs

topics.title: Actions & Events
topics.contentHtml:
C# Events and Async Patterns for Godot Developers

Understanding Events, Actions, and Async Patterns in .NET

Table of Contents

Events/Actions = Godot Signals

The Observer Pattern Connection

Understanding async void

Complete Comparison Reference

Practical Implementation

Events/Actions = Godot Signals {#events-are-signals}

Direct Comparison: Godot Signal vs C# Event

Events in C# are exactly like Signals in Godot - they implement the same Observer pattern for decoupled communication between objects.

In Godot (GDScript):

# Define a signal

signal health_changed(new_health)

# Emit the signal

emit_signal("health_changed", 50)

# Connect to the signal

player.connect("health_changed", self, "_on_player_health_changed")

func _on_player_health_changed(new_health):

    print("Health is now: ", new_health)

In C# (Events):

// Define an event (like a signal)

public event Action<int> OnHealthChanged;

// Fire the event (like emit_signal)

OnHealthChanged?.Invoke(50);

// Subscribe to the event (like connect)

player.OnHealthChanged += OnPlayerHealthChanged;

private void OnPlayerHealthChanged(int newHealth)

{

    Console.WriteLine($"Health is now: {newHealth}");

}

Understanding Action Types

Action is a delegate type (function pointer) that defines what parameters the signal/event sends:

// Godot signal with parameters

signal item_picked_up(item_name, quantity)  // Sends string and int

// C# equivalent

public event Action<string, int> OnItemPickedUp;  // Action<string, int> = sends string and int

Common Action Types:

Action Type Parameters Godot Equivalent
Action None signal clicked()
Action<int> One integer signal health_changed(amount)
Action<string, int> String and integer signal item_picked(name, qty)
Action<CrmEmpresa> Complex object signal company_changed(company_data)

The Observer Pattern Connection {#observer-pattern}

Events and Signals are implementations of the Observer Pattern, providing loose coupling between components.

Pattern Structure:

// THE PATTERN:

// Subject (Observable) ← Has the event

// Observers (Listeners) ← Subscribe to the event

// In practice:

public class ThemeChangeService  // Subject (like a Godot Node with signals)

{

    public event Action<CrmEmpresa> OnThemeChanged;  // The signal



    public void NotifyThemeChanged(CrmEmpresa empresa)

    {

        OnThemeChanged?.Invoke(empresa);  // emit_signal()

    }

}

public class MainLayout  // Observer (like a Godot Node listening to signals)

{

    void Subscribe()

    {

        service.OnThemeChanged += HandleChange;  // connect()

    }



    void HandleChange(CrmEmpresa empresa)  // Signal handler

    {

        // React to the signal

    }



    void Unsubscribe()

    {

        service.OnThemeChanged -= HandleChange;  // disconnect()

    }

}

Understanding async void {#async-void}

Why async void is Usually Bad

The main issue with async void is exception handling and error propagation.

Normal async method (Good):

public async Task SaveDataAsync()  // Returns Task

{

    await DatabaseSave();

    // If this crashes, the Task contains the exception

    // Caller can catch it

}

// Usage:

try 

{

    await SaveDataAsync();  // Can catch exceptions!

}

catch(Exception ex)

{

    // We can handle errors

}

Async void method (Dangerous):

public async void SaveDataAsync()  // Returns nothing

{

    await DatabaseSave();

    // If this crashes, exception goes to global handler

    // Can CRASH your entire app!

}

// Usage:

SaveDataAsync(); // Can't await it! Can't catch exceptions!

// If it fails, your app might crash

Why Events MUST Use async void

Events are defined to return void, not Task, because they follow a fire-and-forget pattern:

// The event delegate signature is fixed:

public event Action<CrmEmpresa> OnThemeChanged;

//            ^^^^^^ 

//            Action returns void, not Task!

// So handlers must match:

async void HandleThemeChanged(CrmEmpresa e)  // Must be void to match Action

{

    try 

    {

        // Always wrap async void in try-catch!

        await DoStuff();

    }

    catch(Exception ex)

    {

        // Handle errors here, don't let them escape!

        _logger.LogError(ex, "Error in event handler");

    }

}

The Godot Analogy

In Godot, signals are fire-and-forget:

# This doesn't wait for handlers

emit_signal("theme_changed", empresa)

# Next line runs immediately

# Similar to C#:

ThemeChangeService.NotifyThemeChanged(empresa);

// Code continues immediately, doesn't wait for handlers

Complete Comparison Reference {#comparison-reference}

Terminology Mapping

Godot C# Purpose
signal event Declare an observable event
emit_signal() Invoke() Fire the event
connect() += Subscribe to event
disconnect() -= Unsubscribe from event
Signal handler Event handler Function that responds
queue_free() Dispose() Cleanup when destroying
AutoLoad singleton Singleton service Global accessible instance
_ready() OnInitialized() Component initialization
_exit_tree() Dispose() Component cleanup

Memory Management Comparison

Godot (Automatic):

func _ready():

    player.connect("health_changed", self, "_on_health_changed")

    # Godot automatically disconnects when node is freed

func _exit_tree():

    # Optional - Godot handles this automatically

    pass

C# (Manual):

protected override void OnInitialized()

{

    player.OnHealthChanged += OnHealthChanged;

    // We MUST manually unsubscribe!

}

public void Dispose()

{

    // REQUIRED - prevent memory leaks!

    player.OnHealthChanged -= OnHealthChanged;

}

Practical Implementation {#practical-implementation}

Complete ThemeChange System Example

If this were Godot:

# ThemeChangeService.gd (like a global AutoLoad)

extends Node

signal theme_changed(company_data)

func notify_theme_changed(company):

    emit_signal("theme_changed", company)

# MainLayout.gd

extends Control

func _ready():

    # Subscribe to the global signal

    ThemeChangeService.connect("theme_changed", self, "_on_theme_changed")

func _on_theme_changed(company):

    # Update UI with new theme

    update_colors(company.color1, company.color2)

    update_logo(company.logo_path)



func _exit_tree():

    # Cleanup (automatic in Godot, manual in C#)

    ThemeChangeService.disconnect("theme_changed", self, "_on_theme_changed")

The C# Implementation:

// ThemeChangeService.cs (Singleton/Scoped service)

public class ThemeChangeService : IThemeChangeService

{

    public event Action<CrmEmpresa> OnThemeChanged;



    public void NotifyThemeChanged(CrmEmpresa empresa)

    {

        OnThemeChanged?.Invoke(empresa);

    }

}

// MainLayout.razor

@implements IDisposable

@code {

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()

    {

        // Subscribe to theme changes (_ready equivalent)

        ThemeChangeService.OnThemeChanged += HandleThemeChanged;

    }



    private async void HandleThemeChanged(CrmEmpresa empresa)

    {

        try

        {

            // Update UI with new theme

            await UpdateColors(empresa.Cor1, empresa.Cor2);

            await UpdateLogo(empresa.LogoNavBar);



            // Tell Blazor to re-render (Godot does this automatically)

            await InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged);

        }

        catch (Exception ex)

        {

            // Always handle exceptions in async void!

            _logger.LogError(ex, "Theme update failed");

        }

    }



    public void Dispose()

    {

        // Manual cleanup required (_exit_tree equivalent)

        ThemeChangeService.OnThemeChanged -= HandleThemeChanged;

    }

}

Thread Safety Considerations

Why InvokeAsync is Needed:

Blazor components are not thread-safe, similar to how Godot's scene tree must be accessed from the main thread:

// Event might fire from any thread

private async void HandleThemeChanged(CrmEmpresa empresa)

{

    // Wrong - might crash if on wrong thread:

    // StateHasChanged();



    // Correct - ensures UI thread:

    await InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged);



    // Similar to Godot's:

    // call_deferred("update_ui")

}

Service Lifetime Comparison

Singleton (Global, like AutoLoad):

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IThemeChangeService, ThemeChangeService>();

// One instance for entire application

// All users share the same instance

// Like Godot's AutoLoad

Scoped (Per-Connection):

builder.Services.AddScoped<IThemeChangeService, ThemeChangeService>();

// One instance per user session

// Each user gets their own instance

// Better for user-specific state

Transient (New Each Time):

builder.Services.AddTransient<IThemeChangeService, ThemeChangeService>();

// New instance every injection

// Rarely used for event systems

Key Takeaways

Events = Signals: C# events are functionally identical to Godot signals

Manual Memory Management: Unlike Godot, C# requires manual event unsubscription

async void Exception: Only use with events, always wrap in try-catch

Thread Safety: Use InvokeAsync() when updating UI from events

Service Lifetimes: Choose Scoped for user-specific events, Singleton for app-wide

Best Practices

Always Implement IDisposable When Using Events:

@implements IDisposable

public void Dispose()

{

    // Unsubscribe all events

    Service.OnEvent -= Handler;

}

Always Handle Exceptions in async void:

private async void EventHandler(Data data)

{

    try

    {

        await AsyncOperation();

    }

    catch (Exception ex)

    {

        _logger.LogError(ex, "Handler failed");

    }

}

Use InvokeAsync for UI Updates:

await InvokeAsync(() =>

{

    // UI updates here

    StateHasChanged();

});

This guide bridges the conceptual gap between Godot's signal system and C#'s event system, helping Godot developers quickly understand and apply C# patterns in their .NET applications.

topics.title: Async Patterns
topics.contentHtml:
Exemplo Microsoft

using System;

using System.Collections.Generic;

using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class Product

{

    public string Name { get; set; }

    public Product(string name)

    {

        Name = name;

    }

}

public class Review

{

    public string Content { get; set; }

    public Review(string content)

    {

        Content = content;

    }

}

public class Program

{

    // Asynchronous method to fetch product data

    public async Task<List<Product>> FetchProductsAsync()

    {

        await Task.Delay(2000); // Simulating a 2-second delay for fetching products

        return new List<Product> 

        { 

            new Product("Eco Bag"), 

            new Product("Reusable Straw") 

        };

    }

    // Asynchronous method to fetch review data

    public async Task<List<Review>> FetchReviewsAsync()

    {

        await Task.Delay(3000); // Simulating a 3-second delay for fetching reviews

        return new List<Review>

        {

            new Review("Great product!"),

            new Review("Good value for the money."),

        };

    }

    // Asynchronous method to display both products and reviews

    public async Task FetchDataAsync()

    {

        // Start fetching products and reviews concurrently

        Task<List<Product>> productsTask = FetchProductsAsync();

        Task<List<Review>> reviewsTask = FetchReviewsAsync();

        // Wait for both tasks to complete

        await Task.WhenAll(productsTask, reviewsTask);

        // Get the results

        List<Product> products = await productsTask;

        List<Review> reviews = await reviewsTask;

        // Display the results

        Console.WriteLine("Products:");

        foreach (Product product in products)

        {

            Console.WriteLine(product.Name);

        }

        // Display fetched reviews

        Console.WriteLine("\nReviews:");

        foreach (Review review in reviews)

        {

            Console.WriteLine(review.Content);

        }

    }

    // Main entry point

    public static async Task Main(string[] args)

    {

        // Calling the asynchronous method to fetch and display products and reviews

        Program program = new Program();

        await program.FetchDataAsync();

    }

}

🔄 These two lines:

Task<List<Product>> productsTask = FetchProductsAsync();

Task<List<Review>> reviewsTask = FetchReviewsAsync();

📌 What they do:They start both asynchronous operations at the same time, but don’t wait for them yet. These methods immediately return a Task that represents the future result of each operation. The actual work (e.g., simulated delays) is already happening in the background.

💡 Think of this like placing two food delivery orders at the same time — you haven’t opened the door yet, but both deliveries are on their way.

🕒 Then:

await Task.WhenAll(productsTask, reviewsTask);

📌 What it does:It tells your program:"Wait here until both deliveries arrive."But importantly: since you started both orders earlier, the timer on both has already been running in parallel.

⏱️ This is way faster than doing:

List<Product> products = await FetchProductsAsync();

List<Review> reviews = await FetchReviewsAsync();

which would first wait 2 seconds for products, then wait another 3 seconds for reviews = 5 seconds total.

With Task.WhenAll, it's just 3 seconds total, since both tasks are running in parallel.

✅ After both are done:

List<Product> products = await productsTask;

List<Review> reviews = await reviewsTask;

📌 What it does:You're now extracting the results (they're already ready at this point). Technically, you could have just used productsTask.Result, but awaiting it is better practice to avoid exceptions being swallowed.

🔁 Summary

Line What it does
Task<List<...>> = Fetch...Async(); Starts async operation (non-blocking).
await Task.WhenAll(...) Waits until both are finished.
await productsTask Retrieves the result. Safe even if already completed.

🧠 TL;DR

You're kicking off two tasks at the same time, then awaiting both with Task.WhenAll, and only then extracting their results. This pattern is how you do real concurrency in C# async — efficient and clean.

If anything's still fuzzy, let me know and I’ll drill into that part further.🧮 Synchronous Example:

int a = Sum(); // This runs Sum()

int b = Sum(); // This runs Sum() again — new call, new result

✅ In this case, each call to Sum() actually runs the method again. So yeah, it's executed twice.

⚡ Asynchronous Example:

Task<List<Product>> productsTask = FetchProductsAsync(); // starts running it ONCE

await Task.WhenAll(productsTask);                         // just waits, doesn’t run it again

List<Product> products = await productsTask; // gets the result of that same run

✅ Here:

FetchProductsAsync() is called once.

productsTask is a reference to that ongoing or completed task.

await productsTask does not call it again — it just waits (if needed) and then unwraps the result.

🧠 Rule of Thumb:

Line Triggers execution?
FetchProductsAsync() ✅ Yes – each call starts a new task
await existingTask ❌ No – just waits for that one to finish and gets its result

So if you write:

var task1 = FetchProductsAsync();

var task2 = FetchProductsAsync();

You’ve actually started two independent tasks, both running the method from scratch.But if you do:

var task = FetchProductsAsync();

await task;

await task;

The second await just gets the same result again — no second call.

🔥 Bottom Line:

Yes — await task doesn’t re-run the method. Only the actual method call (FetchProductsAsync()) creates a new execution.

Exemplo do Gepeto

public async Task DoWorkAsync()

{

    // Moment 1: Start the task

    Task<int> dataTask = GetDataAsync();

    // Meanwhile, do other work in parallel

    DoOtherWork();

    await Task.Delay(5000); // simulate 5 seconds of unrelated work

    // Moment 15: Await the result when actually needed

    int result = await dataTask;

    Console.WriteLine($"Data result: {result}");

}

private async Task<int> GetDataAsync()

{

    await Task.Delay(10000); // simulate long fetch

    return 42;

}How it works:

At “moment 1” → GetDataAsync() starts running immediately because we assigned it to dataTask.

The returned Task<int> represents a promise of the future result.

The code keeps running without blocking.

At “moment 15” → we await dataTask to get the actual result, and if it’s already completed, the await resumes immediately.

Benefits:

Overlaps the long-running task with other work.

Reduces idle waiting time.

Keeps code clean and non-blocking.

Pitfalls to watch for:

If you forget to await the task at some point, you may swallow exceptions silently (unless you handle them from the task itself).

If the task’s result is needed sooner than expected, you could still end up waiting the full duration.

💡 Key Insight
async/await doesn't create new threads — it releases the current thread back to the pool while waiting for I/O. This is crucial for server scalability.
✅ Golden Rules
  • Always use async Task, never async void (except event handlers)
  • Don't use .Result or .Wait() — they cause deadlocks in ASP.NET
  • Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
  • Always pass CancellationToken through async chains

phases.name: Building with Blazor
phases.subtitle: Framework Essentials
phases.description: Server-side Blazor, cookies, JS interop, and data loading.

topics.title: Blazor Fundamentals
topics.contentHtml:
What is Blazor?

Blazor is a framework for building interactive web UIs using C# instead of JavaScript. It runs on .NET and lets you share code between server and client.

💡 Key Insight
Blazor lets C# developers build full-stack web apps without writing JavaScript. Components are .razor files that mix HTML markup with C# code.

Server vs WebAssembly

FeatureBlazor ServerBlazor WASM
ExecutionServer-side, DOM diffs via SignalRClient-side, runs in browser
Initial LoadFast (small download)Slower (download .NET runtime)
OfflineNo (requires connection)Yes (after cached)
Server ResourcesMemory per user (circuit)Minimal server load
LatencyEvery UI event → server round-tripInstant (local execution)

Component Lifecycle

@page "/counter"

<h3>Count: @count</h3>
<button @onclick="Increment">Click me</button>

@code {
    private int count = 0;

    // Called when component is first initialized
    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        // Load data from services
        await LoadData();
    }

    // Called after each render
    protected override void OnAfterRender(bool firstRender)
    {
        if (firstRender)
        {
            // JS interop calls go here
        }
    }

    private void Increment() => count++;
}
✅ Golden Rule
OnInitializedAsync runs once when the component loads. OnParametersSetAsync runs when parent passes new parameters. OnAfterRender runs after the DOM updates — use it for JS interop.

Key Concepts

  • Parameters — Data passed from parent to child via [Parameter] attributes
  • EventCallback — Child-to-parent communication (like events in WPF)
  • Cascading Values — Data that flows down the component tree without explicit passing
  • RenderFragment — Allows components to accept child content (like slots in Vue)
  • Dependency Injection — Services injected via @inject directive

topics.title: Blazor Architecture & Security
topics.contentHtml:
Blazor Server Internals

Circuits

Each user connection creates a circuit — a server-side unit that holds the component tree, state, and service instances. When a user interacts with the page, UI events travel over SignalR to the server, which processes them and sends back DOM diffs.

💡 Key Insight
A circuit is essentially a "virtual browser tab" on the server. All your C# component code, event handlers, and DI-scoped services live in this circuit. If the SignalR connection drops, the circuit stays alive briefly (configurable) waiting for reconnection.

SignalR Transport

Blazor Server uses SignalR WebSockets as its primary transport. The connection is persistent — every button click, text input, and dropdown selection sends a message to the server. The server processes the event, re-renders affected components, and sends a minimal diff back.

Prerendering

// In _Host.cshtml
<component type="typeof(App)" render-mode="ServerPrerendered" />

// ServerPrerendered = HTML rendered on server first (SEO friendly),
// then Blazor takes over when SignalR connects.
// Warning: OnInitializedAsync runs TWICE with prerendering!
⚠️ Common Pitfall
With ServerPrerendered, lifecycle methods run twice — once during prerender (no JS interop available!) and once when the circuit connects. Guard JS interop calls with firstRender checks in OnAfterRender.

Security Model

  • Authentication State — Provided via AuthenticationStateProvider, cascaded down the tree
  • AuthorizeView — Component that conditionally renders based on auth state
  • Circuit isolation — Each user's circuit is separate; no cross-circuit data leaks
  • Anti-forgery — SignalR messages are inherently protected (no CSRF on WebSocket)
✅ Golden Rule
Never trust the client. Even though Blazor Server runs C# on the server, always validate at the service layer. The UI is just a presentation layer — authorization checks belong in your services.

topics.title: Cookie Handling in Blazor Server
topics.contentHtml:
Cookie Handling in Blazor Server Applications

Understanding the Prerendering Cookie Problem and Solution

Executive Summary

This document explains how we solved a critical authentication issue in a Blazor Server application where users couldn't access pages directly via URL, but navigation within the app worked fine. The root cause was a mismatch in how cookies are handled during prerendering versus normal operation.

The Problem

Symptoms

❌ Direct URL access (e.g., example.com/Dashboard) → Redirect loop to login

✅ Navigation within app → Works perfectly

❌ Refresh page (F5) → Redirect loop to login

✅ Click menu link → Works perfectly

Root Cause

Cookies were being handled differently by two systems:

JavaScript - Returns cookies exactly as stored

ASP.NET HttpContext - Automatically URL-decodes cookies

This mismatch caused decryption failures during prerendering, making the app think users weren't authenticated.

Understanding Cookie Flow

1. Setting a Cookie (Login Process)

User Login → Create Session → Serialize to JSON → Encrypt → URL Encode → Store Cookie

Step-by-step transformation:

Step Action Example Data
1 User logs in Username: "Admin", Company: "ACME Corp"
2 Create session object {User: {Id: 1, Name: "Admin"}, Company: {Id: 1}}
3 Serialize to JSON '{"User":{"Id":1,"Name":"Admin"}}'
4 Encrypt (AES) "x7B2mK+3/4Qz==" (Base64)
5 URL Encode "x7B2mK%2B3%2F4Qz%3D%3D"
6 Store in cookie document.cookie = "user=x7B2mK%2B3%2F4Qz%3D%3D"

Why URL Encoding?

  • becomes %2B

/ becomes %2F

= becomes %3D

This ensures special characters don't break the cookie storage.

2. Reading a Cookie - Two Different Methods

Method A: JavaScript (After Page Loads)

getCookie("user")

// Returns: "x7B2mK%2B3%2F4Qz%3D%3D" (still URL-encoded)

When this happens:

After page is fully rendered

User clicks navigation links

Any client-side interaction

Method B: ASP.NET HttpContext (During Prerendering)

HttpContext.Request.Cookies["user"]

// Returns: "x7B2mK+3/4Qz==" (automatically URL-decoded!)

When this happens:

Direct URL access

Page refresh (F5)

Initial page load

The Critical Difference

Source Returns URL Decoded?
JavaScript getCookie() "x7B2mK%2B3%2F4Qz%3D%3D" No
HttpContext "x7B2mK+3/4Qz==" Yes (automatic)

Why It Broke

The Decryption Method Expected URL-Encoded Input

public static string Decrypt(string cipherText)

{

    // Step 1: URL decode

    string base64 = HttpUtility.UrlDecode(cipherText);

    // Step 2: Decrypt the base64...

}

The Double-Decode Problem

When ASP.NET already decoded the cookie:

Input: "x7B2mK+3/4Qz==" (already decoded by ASP.NET)

    ↓

UrlDecode(): Tries to decode again

    ↓

Result: Corrupted data

    ↓

Error: "Invalid Base64 string"

    ↓

Authentication fails

    ↓

Redirect to login

The Solution

1. Add HttpContextAccessor for Prerendering Support

// Program.cs

builder.Services.AddHttpContextAccessor();

builder.Services.AddScoped<ISessionService, SessionService>();

2. Modify SessionService Constructor

public class SessionService : ISessionService

{

    private readonly IHttpContextAccessor _httpContextAccessor;



    public SessionService(

        IJSRuntime jsRuntime,

        IHttpContextAccessor httpContextAccessor) // NEW!

    {

        _httpContextAccessor = httpContextAccessor;

    }

}

3. Create Flexible Decryption Method

private string DecryptData(string cookieValue, bool skipUrlDecode = false)

{

    // Handle both encoded and decoded cookies

    string base64 = skipUrlDecode 

        ? cookieValue                          // Already decoded by ASP.NET

        : HttpUtility.UrlDecode(cookieValue);  // Needs decoding from JS



    // Continue with decryption...

    using (var aes = Aes.Create())

    {

        // ... decrypt base64 ...

    }

}

4. Update GetUserSessionAsync

public async Task<EmpresaUserSession> GetUserSessionAsync()

{

    // Check memory first (fastest)

    if (_sessionData.ContainsKey("user"))

        return (EmpresaUserSession)_sessionData["user"];



    // During prerendering - use HttpContext

    if (_httpContextAccessor?.HttpContext != null)

    {

        var cookieValue = _httpContextAccessor.HttpContext.Request.Cookies["user"];

        if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(cookieValue))

        {

            // HttpContext auto-decoded it, so skip URL decode

            var session = DecryptData(cookieValue, skipUrlDecode: true);

            if (session != null)

            {

                _sessionData["user"] = session;

                return session;

            }

        }

    }



    // After rendering - use JavaScript

    try

    {

        var cookieValue = await GetCookieAsync("user");

        if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(cookieValue))

        {

            // JS returns raw cookie, needs URL decode

            var session = DecryptData(cookieValue, skipUrlDecode: false);

            if (session != null)

            {

                _sessionData["user"] = session;

                return session;

            }

        }

    }

    catch (InvalidOperationException ex) when (ex.Message.Contains("JavaScript interop"))

    {

        // Expected during prerendering - JavaScript not available yet

        return null;

    }



    return null;

}

The Complete Flow

Before Fix (Broken)

1. User accesses example.com/Dashboard

    ↓

2. Prerendering starts (no JavaScript)

    ↓

3. Try to read cookie via HttpContext

    ↓

4. Cookie is auto-decoded: "x7B2mK+3/4Qz=="

    ↓

5. Decrypt tries to URL-decode again

    ↓

6. ❌ ERROR: Invalid Base64

    ↓

7. No session found

    ↓

8. Redirect to /Login

    ↓

9. Login page checks cookie (same problem)

    ↓

10. Redirect loop!

After Fix (Working)

1. User accesses example.com/Dashboard

    ↓

2. Prerendering starts (no JavaScript)

    ↓

3. Try to read cookie via HttpContext

    ↓

4. Cookie is auto-decoded: "x7B2mK+3/4Qz=="

    ↓

5. Decrypt with skipUrlDecode=true

    ↓

6. ✅ SUCCESS: Valid session found

    ↓

7. Page loads normally

Key Concepts Explained

What is Prerendering?

Blazor Server can render pages in two phases:

Prerendering - Server generates initial HTML before establishing WebSocket connection

Interactive - After WebSocket connection, full interactivity with JavaScript

What is HttpContext?

Contains all information about the current HTTP request

Includes headers, cookies, user info, query strings

Only available server-side

Available during prerendering (before JavaScript loads)

What is HttpContextAccessor?

A service that provides access to HttpContext

Must be registered in dependency injection

Allows services to access HTTP request information

The Cookie Encoding Journey

Stage Encoding Example
Original Plain text Hello+World/=
URL Encoded Special chars replaced Hello%2BWorld%2F%3D
In Cookie URL encoded Hello%2BWorld%2F%3D
JS reads Still encoded Hello%2BWorld%2F%3D
HttpContext reads Auto-decoded Hello+World/=

Best Practices Learned

1. Always Consider Prerendering

When building Blazor Server apps, always test:

Direct URL access

Page refresh

In-app navigation

2. Handle Both Cookie Sources

// Good practice: Check both sources

if (IsPrerendering)

    ReadFromHttpContext();

else

    ReadFromJavaScript();

3. Centralize Session Management

Keep all session/cookie logic in one service for easier maintenance.

4. Log the Source

_logger.LogDebug("Reading cookie from: {Source}", 

    _httpContextAccessor != null ? "HttpContext" : "JavaScript");

Troubleshooting Guide

Symptom: Redirect Loop

Check: Is cookie being read correctly during prerendering? Solution: Ensure HttpContextAccessor is registered and used

Symptom: "Invalid Base64" Errors

Check: Is cookie being double-decoded? Solution: Use skipUrlDecode parameter based on source

Symptom: Works in Development, Not Production

Check: HTTPS settings and cookie security flags Solution: Ensure cookie settings match environment

Symptom: Session Lost on Refresh

Check: Is session only stored in memory? Solution: Ensure cookie persistence is working

Summary

The core issue was that ASP.NET automatically URL-decodes cookies when reading them via HttpContext, but JavaScript returns them exactly as stored. Our decryption method expected URL-encoded input, so when it received already-decoded data from HttpContext, it would fail.

The solution was to:

Add HttpContextAccessor to read cookies during prerendering

Create a flexible decryption method that can handle both encoded and decoded input

Detect the source of the cookie and apply the appropriate decryption strategy

This ensures authentication works correctly whether users:

Navigate within the app (JavaScript)

Access pages directly via URL (HttpContext)

Refresh pages (HttpContext then JavaScript)

Appendix: Related Code Files

Services/Session/SessionService.cs - Main session management

Data/Encrypter.cs - Encryption/decryption logic (now integrated into SessionService)

Pages/_Host.cshtml - JavaScript cookie functions

Shared/AuthenticatedComponentBase.cs - Base class for authenticated pages

Program.cs - Service registration

topics.title: JS Interop & Static Events
topics.contentHtml:
Blazor JS Interop: Static Events vs Instance-Isolated Callbacks

Level: Advanced
Topic: Blazor Server + JavaScript Interop Race Conditions

The Problem

When Blazor components need to receive callbacks from JavaScript, a common pattern is using static events:

// Static helper class
public static class MyHelper
{
    public static event Action<string>? OnDataReceived;

    [JSInvokable]
    public static void NotifyDataReceived(string data)
    {
        OnDataReceived?.Invoke(data);
    }
}
// JavaScript
DotNet.invokeMethodAsync('MyApp', 'NotifyDataReceived', data);

This works perfectly when only ONE component is active. But when multiple component instances exist simultaneously (e.g., two kiosks, two browser tabs), all subscribers receive all events.

The Bug: Data Leakage Between Concurrent Users

Scenario

Two facial recognition kiosks running simultaneously:

Kiosk A (Component Instance #1)
├── Subscribes to: FacialRecognitionHelper.OnFacialIdentifyComplete
└── User Alice approaches and scans face

Kiosk B (Component Instance #2)
├── Subscribes to: FacialRecognitionHelper.OnFacialIdentifyComplete (SAME EVENT!)
└── User Bob approaches and scans face

Timeline of Bug

T0: Alice's face detected    → JS calls NotifyFacialIdentifyComplete(aliceDescriptor)
T1: Static event broadcasts to ALL subscribers
T2: BOTH Kiosk A and Kiosk B receive Alice's descriptor
T3: Both kiosks call IdentifyUserForAttendanceAsync(aliceDescriptor)
T4: Both kiosks display "Welcome, Alice!" (BOB SEES ALICE'S DATA!)

T5: Bob's face detected     → JS calls NotifyFacialIdentifyComplete(bobDescriptor)
T6: BOTH kiosks receive Bob's descriptor
T7: BOTH kiosks now show "Welcome, Bob!" (ALICE'S SCREEN CHANGES!)

Diagram: Broadcast Problem

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        JAVASCRIPT (face-api.js)                      │
│                                                                       │
│  Face Detected → DotNet.invokeMethodAsync('NotifyFacialIdentify')   │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    STATIC HELPER (C#)                                │
│                                                                       │
│  [JSInvokable]                                                       │
│  public static void NotifyFacialIdentifyComplete(string descriptor)  │
│  {                                                                   │
│      OnFacialIdentifyComplete?.Invoke(descriptor);  // BROADCASTS!  │
│  }                                                                   │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
              ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
              │                                  │
              ▼                                  ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│      KIOSK A            │      │      KIOSK B            │
│  OnIdentifyComplete()   │      │  OnIdentifyComplete()   │
│  _employee = Alice      │      │  _employee = Alice (!)  │
│                         │      │  (Should be Bob!)       │
└─────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────┘

The Solution: Instance-Isolated Callbacks

Instead of broadcasting to all subscribers, route events to the specific component instance that initiated the action.

Pattern Overview

1. Component generates unique instanceId (Guid)
2. Component registers its callback with the helper using instanceId
3. Component passes instanceId to JavaScript when starting capture
4. JavaScript includes instanceId when calling back to .NET
5. Helper routes callback ONLY to the registered instance
6. Component unregisters in Dispose()

Implementation

1. Static Helper with Instance Registry

public static class FacialRecognitionHelper
{
    // Instance-specific callbacks (thread-safe)
    private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Action<string>> _identifyCallbacks = new();

    // Register instance callback
    public static void RegisterInstance(string instanceId, Action<string> onIdentify)
    {
        _identifyCallbacks[instanceId] = onIdentify;
    }

    // Unregister on dispose
    public static void UnregisterInstance(string instanceId)
    {
        _identifyCallbacks.TryRemove(instanceId, out _);
    }

    // Instance-specific callback (NEW - routes to specific instance)
    [JSInvokable]
    public static void NotifyFacialIdentifyCompleteForInstance(string instanceId, string descriptor)
    {
        if (_identifyCallbacks.TryGetValue(instanceId, out var callback))
        {
            callback.Invoke(descriptor);
        }
    }
}

2. Component with Instance ID

@code {
    private readonly string _instanceId = Guid.NewGuid().ToString();

    protected override void OnInitialized()
    {
        // Register this instance's callback
        FacialRecognitionHelper.RegisterInstance(_instanceId, HandleIdentifyComplete);
    }

    private async Task StartCapture()
    {
        // Pass instanceId to JavaScript
        await JS.InvokeVoidAsync("facialRecognition.startIdentify",
            _videoElementId, _canvasContainerId, _instanceId);
    }

    public void Dispose()
    {
        FacialRecognitionHelper.UnregisterInstance(_instanceId);
    }
}

3. JavaScript with Instance Routing

let currentInstanceId = null;

async function startFacialAttendance(videoElementId, canvasContainerId, mode, instanceId) {
    currentInstanceId = instanceId;

    // ... face detection code ...

    // When face is detected, call back with instanceId
    if (currentInstanceId) {
        await DotNet.invokeMethodAsync('HRModule',
            'NotifyFacialIdentifyCompleteForInstance',
            currentInstanceId,
            descriptorJson);
    }
}

Diagram: Instance-Isolated Solution

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        JAVASCRIPT (face-api.js)                      │
│                                                                       │
│  startIdentify(videoId, canvasId, instanceId="abc-123")             │
│  ↓                                                                   │
│  Face Detected → NotifyFacialIdentifyCompleteForInstance(           │
│                      "abc-123",    ← Instance ID                     │
│                      descriptor)                                      │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    STATIC HELPER (C#)                                │
│                                                                       │
│  _identifyCallbacks = {                                              │
│      "abc-123": KioskA.HandleIdentify,                               │
│      "def-456": KioskB.HandleIdentify                                │
│  }                                                                   │
│                                                                       │
│  NotifyFacialIdentifyCompleteForInstance("abc-123", descriptor)      │
│  → Routes ONLY to Kiosk A's callback                                 │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│      KIOSK A            │      │      KIOSK B            │
│  instanceId = "abc-123" │      │  instanceId = "def-456" │
│  HandleIdentify() ✓     │      │  (not called)          │
│  _employee = Alice      │      │  _employee = Bob        │
└─────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────┘

When to Use Each Pattern

Static Events (Broadcast) - OK When:

  • Only ONE component instance will ever exist
  • All components should receive all events (rare)
  • The callback is truly global (app-level notifications)

Instance-Isolated Callbacks - Required When:

  • Multiple component instances may be active simultaneously
  • Each instance should only receive its own events
  • User data must be isolated between sessions
  • Security/privacy is important

Key Takeaways

  1. Static events are shared - All subscribers receive all events
  2. Instance IDs provide isolation - Each component gets only its events
  3. ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe - Multiple registrations are safe
  4. Always unregister in Dispose() - Prevent memory leaks
  5. JavaScript must track the instanceId - Pass it through the entire flow

Related Files

  • FacialRecognitionHelper.cs
  • FacialAttendanceComponent.razor
  • script.js
topics.forDummiesHtml:
Static Events Problem - For Dummies

A simple explanation of why two kiosk users were seeing each other's data

The Loudspeaker Analogy

Imagine you're in an office building with a loudspeaker system.

The Problem: One Loudspeaker for Everyone

When the receptionist calls "John Smith, your package is here!" over the loudspeaker:

   📢 LOUDSPEAKER: "John Smith, your package is here!"
       │
       ├──► Office A hears it
       ├──► Office B hears it
       ├──► Office C hears it
       └──► EVERYONE hears it!

Now imagine TWO receptionists using the SAME loudspeaker:

Receptionist 1: "John Smith, your package!"
Receptionist 2: "Maria Garcia, your package!"

   📢 LOUDSPEAKER broadcasts BOTH messages
       │
       ├──► John hears his message ✓
       ├──► John ALSO hears Maria's message ✗
       ├──► Maria hears her message ✓
       └──► Maria ALSO hears John's message ✗

This is exactly what was happening with our facial recognition kiosks!

What Happened in Our App

Before (The Bug)

   Kiosk A (Alice scanning her face)
       │
       └──► "Face detected!" ────┐
                                  │
                                  ▼
                         📢 BROADCAST to EVERYONE
                                  │
       ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┐
       │                                                      │
       ▼                                                      ▼
   Kiosk A                                               Kiosk B
   Shows: "Welcome, Alice!"                              Shows: "Welcome, Alice!"
                                                         (But BOB is standing there!)

Both kiosks received Alice's identification, even though Bob was at Kiosk B!

After (The Fix)

   Kiosk A (Alice)                    Kiosk B (Bob)
   ID: "abc-123"                      ID: "xyz-789"
       │                                  │
       └──► "Face detected!"              └──► "Face detected!"
            + ID: "abc-123"                    + ID: "xyz-789"
                │                                  │
                ▼                                  ▼
         📬 MAILBOX "abc-123"              📬 MAILBOX "xyz-789"
         (Only Alice's kiosk)              (Only Bob's kiosk)
                │                                  │
                ▼                                  ▼
         "Welcome, Alice!"                 "Welcome, Bob!"

Now each kiosk has its own "mailbox" (instance ID). Messages only go to the right kiosk!

Visual Summary

Before: Loudspeaker (Broken)

  👤 Alice                    👤 Bob
     │                           │
     │                           │
   ┌─┴─────────────────────────┬─┴─┐
   │     📢 SHARED SPEAKER      │   │
   │   "Alice identified!"      │   │
   └─────────────────────────────────┘
          │           │
          ▼           ▼
       ✅ Alice    ❌ Bob sees Alice!

After: Private Mailboxes (Fixed)

  👤 Alice                    👤 Bob
     │                           │
   📬 abc-123                  📬 xyz-789
     │                           │
     ▼                           ▼
  ✅ Alice                    ✅ Bob

The One-Sentence Explanation

Old way: Shouting into a megaphone (everyone hears everything)
New way: Sending private text messages (only the right person receives)

Key Takeaway

When multiple users might do the same thing at the same time, each user needs their own private channel - not a shared broadcast.

For the technical details, see 06-Blazor-JS-Interop-Static-Events.md

topics.title: EF Core: Loadings, Includes & Virtuals
topics.contentHtml:
📘 Entity Framework Core — Relationships, Lazy Loading & Virtual Properties

🧩 1. Navigation Properties & Foreign Keys

In EF Core, each relationship usually uses both an FK property and a navigation property:


public class Empresa

{

    public string EmpresaId { get; set; }

    public string Nome { get; set; }

    // Foreign key

    public int CountryId { get; set; }

    // Navigation property

    public Country Country { get; set; }

}
Property Purpose Stored in DB?
----------- ---------- ---------------
CountryId Foreign key, links entities ✅ Yes
Country Navigation for related data ❌ No

⚙️ 2. Loading Related Data

Loading type Description Example SQL queries Recommended for
--------------- -------------- ---------- -------------- -----------------
Lazy Loading Loads data when property is first accessed empresa.Country.Name Many (N+1) Small datasets, simple UIs
Eager Loading Loads related data up front via join .Include(e => e.Country) Single Lists, tables, APIs
Explicit Loading Manually load related data later context.Entry(e).Reference(x => x.Country).Load() Separate Controlled cases

🧠 3. The virtual Keyword

Context Is virtual needed? Why
---------- ---------------------- -----
Lazy loading ✅ Yes EF substitutes proxy overrides for navigation props
Eager loading (Include) ❌ No Data loaded via join
Explicit loading (Load) ❌ No Manual load
Projection (Select) ❌ No Custom object mapping
💡 Tip: Many production apps turn lazy loading off for predictable performance and simpler debugging.

🧱 4. Recommended Relationship Setup


public class Country

{

    public int CountryId { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }

    public ICollection<Empresa> Empresas { get; set; }

}

public class Empresa

{

    public string EmpresaId { get; set; }

    public string Nome { get; set; }

    public int CountryId { get; set; }

    public Country Country { get; set; }

}

Optional explicit Fluent API configuration:


modelBuilder.Entity<Empresa>()

    .HasOne(e => e.Country)

    .WithMany(c => c.Empresas)

    .HasForeignKey(e => e.CountryId);

🚀 5. Query Examples

✅ Eager Loading (Recommended for lists)


var empresas = dbContext.Empresas

    .Include(e => e.Country)

    .Select(e => new

    {

        e.EmpresaId,

        e.Nome,

        CountryName = e.Country.Name

    })

    .ToList();

🧠 Result: A single optimized JOIN query fetching only needed data.

🧰 6. [NotMapped] Attribute

Use [NotMapped] only for properties that don’t exist in the database, e.g.:


[NotMapped]

public string DisplayName => $"{Nome} ({Country?.Name})";

Do not use [NotMapped] on valid navigation properties like Country.

⚡ 7. Performance Tips

Tip Why
----- -----
Avoid lazy loading in large loops Prevents N+1 query issues
Use .Include() Loads related data in one query
Use .Select() Fetch only columns you need
Keep virtual only if lazy loading is used Otherwise unnecessary
Turn off lazy loading globally in production Makes query flow explicit

🧭 8. Quick Decision Guide

Scenario Lazy Loading Eager Loading virtual Needed [NotMapped]
----------- --------------- --------------- ------------------ ---------------
Small admin pages ✅ Optional ✅ Good ✅ Yes ❌ No
Large tables / APIs ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ No ❌ No
Computed property N/A N/A ❌ No ✅ Yes
DTO / projection ❌ No ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ (if outside EF)

✅ 9. Key Takeaways

  • ✔️ Keep both CountryId (FK) and Country (navigation).
  • ⚙️ Use .Include() or .Select() instead of lazy loading.
  • 🚫 Don’t mark navigation properties [NotMapped].
  • 🧠 Only use virtual when you enable lazy loading.
  • 💪 Prefer eager loading for predictable, performant queries.
  • 🧾 EF automatically manages relationships via conventions or OnModelCreating.

End of Notes — EF Core Relationship & Loading Reference

💡 Eager vs Lazy Loading
Eager (.Include()): loads related data in one query. Use when you know you'll need the data.
Lazy (virtual properties): loads on first access. Beware N+1 queries!
Explicit (.Entry().Collection().Load()): you control exactly when to load.

phases.name: Thinking in Layers
phases.subtitle: Architecture & Code Quality
phases.description: Why code is structured the way it is.

topics.title: Clean Architecture
topics.contentHtml:
Understanding Clean Architecture

What is Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture separates your application into layers, where each layer has a specific responsibility. The key principle is that dependencies point inward - outer layers depend on inner layers, never the reverse.

HRModule Architecture Layers

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    UI LAYER                              │
│  (Razor Pages, Components)                               │
│  - Displays data                                         │
│  - Handles user input                                    │
│  - Calls services                                        │
│  - NO business logic                                     │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ depends on
                         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  SERVICE LAYER                           │
│  (IEmployeeService, IAuthorizationService, etc.)         │
│  - ALL business logic                                    │
│  - Validation                                            │
│  - Orchestration                                         │
│  - Returns ServiceResult<T>                              │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                         │ depends on
                         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   DATA LAYER                             │
│  (DbContext, Models)                                     │
│  - Database access                                       │
│  - Entity definitions                                    │
│  - EF Core configurations                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Golden Rules

1. UI Layer: Display Only

<!-- GOOD: UI just displays and calls service -->
@inject IEmployeeService EmployeeService

<MudText>@employee.Nome</MudText>
<MudButton OnClick="SaveEmployee">Guardar</MudButton>

@code {
    private async Task SaveEmployee()
    {
        var result = await EmployeeService.UpdateEmployeeAsync(employee);
        if (!result.Success) Snackbar.Add(result.Message, Severity.Error);
    }
}
<!-- BAD: Business logic in UI -->
@code {
    private async Task SaveEmployee()
    {
        // DON'T DO THIS - validation belongs in service
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(employee.Nome))
        {
            Snackbar.Add("Nome obrigatorio", Severity.Error);
            return;
        }

        // DON'T DO THIS - DB access belongs in service
        await _context.Funcionarios.AddAsync(employee);
        await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}

2. Service Layer: All Business Logic

// GOOD: Business logic in service
public class EmployeeService : IEmployeeService
{
    public async Task<ServiceResult<CrmFuncionario>> UpdateEmployeeAsync(
        EmpresaUserSession session,
        CrmFuncionario employee)
    {
        // Validation
        if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(employee.Nome))
            return ServiceResult<CrmFuncionario>.Failure("Nome obrigatorio");

        // Business rules
        if (employee.DataNascimento > DateTime.Today)
            return ServiceResult<CrmFuncionario>.Failure("Data invalida");

        // Database operation
        await using var context = await _contextFactory.CreateDbContextAsync(session.CompanyDatabase);
        context.Funcionarios.Update(employee);
        await context.SaveChangesAsync();

        // Audit
        await _auditService.LogAsync(session.User.Id, $"Updated employee {employee.Id}");

        return ServiceResult<CrmFuncionario>.Success(employee);
    }
}

3. ServiceResult Pattern

Always return results with success/failure status:

public class ServiceResult<T>
{
    public bool Success { get; set; }
    public string Message { get; set; }
    public T? Data { get; set; }

    public static ServiceResult<T> Success(T data) => new() { Success = true, Data = data };
    public static ServiceResult<T> Failure(string message) => new() { Success = false, Message = message };
}

Why This Matters

Testability

Services can be unit tested without UI:

[Test]
public async Task UpdateEmployee_InvalidName_ReturnsFailure()
{
    var service = new EmployeeService(mockContext, mockAudit);
    var result = await service.UpdateEmployeeAsync(session, new CrmFuncionario { Nome = "" });
    Assert.IsFalse(result.Success);
}

Maintainability

  • Change business rules in one place (service)
  • UI changes don't affect logic
  • Easy to find where logic lives

Reusability

Same service can be used by:

  • Web UI (Blazor)
  • API endpoints
  • Background jobs
  • Other services

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake Problem Fix
LINQ in Razor Logic in UI Move to service
DbContext in component Direct DB access Inject service
Validation in UI Duplicated logic Validate in service
Complex @code blocks Too much UI logic Extract to service

topics.title: Polite Code Style
topics.contentHtml:
Polite Code Style Guide

What is "Polite Code"?

Polite code is self-documenting, readable, and expressive. Instead of forcing developers to trace through complex logic, polite code tells you exactly what it does at a glance.

Key Principles

1. Boolean Properties with Clear Names

// GOOD - "Polite" boolean properties
protected bool IsSuperAdmin => RoleLevel >= 100;
protected bool IsAdminOrAbove => RoleLevel >= 80;
protected bool IsManagerOrAbove => RoleLevel >= 60;
protected bool HasLinkedEmployee => employeeLinkage != null && employeeLinkage.IsActive;

// BAD - Unclear
protected bool CheckAdmin() => role > 2;
protected bool HasEmployee => emp != null;

2. Compound Conditions That Read Like English

// GOOD - Reads like a sentence: "If admin or above AND employee belongs to current company AND has linked employee ID"
@if (IsAdminOrAbove && colaboradorBelongsToCurrentCompany && LinkedEmployeeId.HasValue)
{
    <EmployeeConfigurationPanel ... />
}

// BAD - Hard to understand at a glance
@if (_role >= 80 && _empCoId == _sessCoId && _linkId != null)
{
    ...
}

3. Descriptive Variable Names

// GOOD
private bool colaboradorBelongsToCurrentCompany = false;
private string? linkedEmployeeCompanyName;
private int? LinkedEmployeeId => employeeLinkage?.EmployeeId;

// BAD
private bool sameCo = false;
private string? empCoName;
private int? empId => link?.EmpId;

4. Properties Over Direct Access

// GOOD - Use properties that express intent
protected int CurrentUserId => UserSession?.User.Id ?? 0;
protected string CompanyDatabase => UserSession?.Empresa?.BaseNome ?? string.Empty;

// Component usage
<SomeComponent UserId="@CurrentUserId" Database="@CompanyDatabase" />

// BAD - Direct access scattered throughout
<SomeComponent UserId="@UserSession?.User.Id ?? 0" Database="@UserSession?.Empresa?.BaseNome ?? string.Empty" />

Real-World Examples from HRModule

Authorization Checks

// In AuthenticatedComponentBase - "Polite" convenience properties
protected bool IsSuperAdmin => RoleLevel >= 100;
protected bool IsAdminOrAbove => RoleLevel >= 80;
protected bool IsManagerOrAbove => RoleLevel >= 60;

// Usage in Razor - crystal clear intent
@if (IsSuperAdmin)
{
    <MudButton Color="Color.Error">Delete System</MudButton>
}

@if (IsAdminOrAbove)
{
    <MudButton>Manage Users</MudButton>
}

@if (IsManagerOrAbove)
{
    <MudButton>View Team Reports</MudButton>
}

Conditional UI Rendering

// UtilizadorDetalhes.razor - All conditions are immediately understandable
@if (IsAdminOrAbove && colaboradorBelongsToCurrentCompany && LinkedEmployeeId.HasValue)
{
    <MudTabPanel Text="Configurações HR" Icon="@Icons.Material.Filled.Settings">
        <EmployeeConfigurationPanel EmployeeId="@LinkedEmployeeId.Value"
                                    CompanyDatabase="@CompanyDatabase"
                                    CurrentUserId="@CurrentUserId"
                                    ReadOnly="@(!IsAdminOrAbove)" />
    </MudTabPanel>
}

Service Methods

// IEmployeeConfigurationService - Method names express exactly what they do
Task<bool> CanEmployeeCheckInAsync(int employeeId, string companyDatabase);
Task<bool> CanEmployeeValidateAttendanceAsync(int employeeId, string companyDatabase);
Task<bool> RequiresGeolocationAsync(int employeeId, string companyDatabase);
Task<bool> HasHoursBankEnabledAsync(int employeeId, string companyDatabase);

Code Review Checklist

When reviewing code, ask:

  1. Readability: Can you understand the condition without tracing variable definitions?
  2. Intent: Does the code express what it's checking, not how?
  3. Naming: Are booleans named as questions that return true/false answers?
  4. Compound Conditions: Do multi-part conditions read like English sentences?
  5. Consistency: Are similar checks using the same patterns throughout?

Migration Strategy

When refactoring existing code to "polite" style:

  1. Identify unclear patterns: Look for magic numbers, abbreviations, direct property chains
  2. Create expressive properties: Add IsXxx, HasXxx, CanXxx properties
  3. Update usages: Replace direct checks with property references
  4. Document intent: Use XML comments for non-obvious properties
// Before
@if (userSession?.User?.Role >= 80 && linkedFuncId != null)

// After - with supporting properties
/// <summary>
/// User has Admin role or higher (SuperAdmin, Admin)
/// </summary>
protected bool IsAdminOrAbove => RoleLevel >= 80;

protected int? LinkedEmployeeId => employeeLinkage?.EmployeeId;

@if (IsAdminOrAbove && LinkedEmployeeId.HasValue)

Summary

Polite code:

  • Uses clear, descriptive names
  • Expresses intent, not implementation
  • Reads like English
  • Is self-documenting
  • Reduces cognitive load for future maintainers

Remember: Code is read far more often than it's written. Invest in readability.

topics.title: Adapter Pattern
topics.contentHtml:
Adapter Pattern Explained

Status: Future implementation - concepts documented for planning

The Problem

Currently, modules are coupled to HRModule-specific data models:

// Jobs module depends on HRModule's CrmFuncionario
public interface IJobService
{
    Task AssignEmployeeToJobAsync(int jobId, CrmFuncionario employee);
}

If we want to reuse the Jobs module in another application that doesn't have CrmFuncionario, it won't work.

The Solution: Adapter Pattern

Each module defines its own interfaces and DTOs. The host application provides adapters that translate between its models and the module's DTOs.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    JOBS MODULE                           │
│  (Portable, doesn't know about CrmFuncionario)           │
│                                                          │
│  interface IEmployeeAdapter                              │
│  {                                                       │
│      Task<EmployeeInfo> GetEmployeeAsync(int id);        │
│  }                                                       │
│                                                          │
│  class EmployeeInfo  // Module's own DTO                 │
│  {                                                       │
│      int Id;                                             │
│      string Name;                                        │
│      string Email;                                       │
│  }                                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          ▲
                          │ implements
                          │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HRMODULE ADAPTER                      │
│  (Translates CrmFuncionario -> EmployeeInfo)             │
│                                                          │
│  class HRModuleEmployeeAdapter : IEmployeeAdapter        │
│  {                                                       │
│      async Task<EmployeeInfo> GetEmployeeAsync(int id)   │
│      {                                                   │
│          var func = await _service.GetByIdAsync(id);     │
│          return new EmployeeInfo                         │
│          {                                               │
│              Id = func.Id,                               │
│              Name = func.Nome,                           │
│              Email = func.Email                          │
│          };                                              │
│      }                                                   │
│  }                                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Before vs After

Before (Coupled)

// Jobs module - DIRECTLY uses CrmFuncionario
public class JobService
{
    private readonly IEmployeeService _employeeService;

    public async Task AssignEmployeeAsync(int jobId, int employeeId)
    {
        CrmFuncionario employee = await _employeeService.GetByIdAsync(employeeId);
        // Uses CrmFuncionario properties directly
        _logger.Log($"Assigned {employee.Nome} to job {jobId}");
    }
}

After (Decoupled)

// Jobs module - Uses its own adapter interface
public class JobService
{
    private readonly IEmployeeAdapter _employeeAdapter;  // Module's interface

    public async Task AssignEmployeeAsync(int jobId, int employeeId)
    {
        EmployeeInfo employee = await _employeeAdapter.GetEmployeeAsync(employeeId);
        // Uses module's own DTO
        _logger.Log($"Assigned {employee.Name} to job {jobId}");
    }
}

// In different app (not HRModule)
public class OtherAppEmployeeAdapter : IEmployeeAdapter
{
    private readonly IWorkerRepository _workerRepo;

    public async Task<EmployeeInfo> GetEmployeeAsync(int id)
    {
        var worker = await _workerRepo.GetAsync(id);
        return new EmployeeInfo
        {
            Id = worker.WorkerId,
            Name = worker.FullName,  // Different property name!
            Email = worker.ContactEmail
        };
    }
}

Benefits

  1. Portability: Modules can be NuGet packages
  2. Independence: Modules don't know about host models
  3. Testability: Mock adapters for unit tests
  4. Flexibility: Different apps provide different adapters

Module Structure (Future)

Modules/
├── Jobs/
│   ├── Jobs.Module.csproj
│   ├── Interfaces/
│   │   └── IEmployeeAdapter.cs
│   ├── DTOs/
│   │   └── EmployeeInfo.cs
│   └── Services/
│       └── JobService.cs
│
└── HRModule.Adapters/
    └── HRModuleEmployeeAdapter.cs

When to Use

Use adapters when:

  • Module needs to be reusable across applications
  • Module should not depend on specific data models
  • Testing requires isolation from real data models

Don't use adapters when:

  • Module is tightly integrated with the application
  • Performance is critical (adapters add overhead)
  • Simple direct dependencies are clearer

Implementation Plan

This pattern is deferred until:

  1. Core schema refactoring is complete and stable
  2. Module boundaries are clearly identified
  3. Adapter interfaces are designed (Interface Segregation)
  4. Gradual migration can be done without breaking functionality
